title: 00 · Privacy and consent system (overview)
description:
# 00 · Privacy and consent system (overview)

Child tickets: 01–14, 16.

## Goal

Keep our cookie policy, ePrivacy/GDPR consent and record keeping correct **by construction**, so two people can keep it up to date without a paid consent-management service. Facts about what the site stores and who it talks to are written down once, in code, and everything else (the policy table, the CSP, consent purges, CI checks) is generated or checked from them.

This is pre-work for adding Google Analytics (or another analytics provider). Google Analytics is treated as already present from the start: it is in the registry, the policy, the CSP and the scans. Turning it on (#14) should then be a configuration change, not a policy change.

## Constraints that shape the design

- The site is static Astro on GitHub Pages: no server, no response headers, no server-side consent log.
- Deploys run from a laptop via `npm run deploy` (`predeploy` builds first). That hook is where checks run.
- localStorage and sessionStorage count the same as cookies under ePrivacy Art. 5(3). The site currently sets **no** first-party cookies.
- Third-party scripts (GA's `gtag.js`) set their own cookies (`_ga`, `_ga_<ID>`) without going through our code. Those are controlled by gating *script loading*, not storage access.
- A request to a third-party origin sends the visitor's IP even with no cookies (a GDPR data transfer), so third-party *origins* are part of the inventory too.

## Architecture: one registry, several enforcement layers

| Layer | What it catches | Ticket |
|---|---|---|
| Registry of categories, vendors and storage keys | The single source of truth | #01 |
| Consent-aware storage interface | First-party writes in a category without consent become no-ops | #02 |
| Lint rule against direct storage access | First-party code bypassing the interface | #03 |
| Consent state + `whenGranted` gate | Third-party scripts loading without consent | #04, #05 |
| Registry lock file with derived version | Disclosure changes that nobody noticed; triggers re-consent | #07, #08 |
| Generated policy table and "Last updated" | Policy drifting from reality | #09 |
| CSP generated from registry origins | Any page contacting an unregistered vendor | #11 |
| Browser scan before every deploy | Ground truth: everything the shipped site actually stores or contacts | #12 |

## Principles

- **Define errors out of existence.** Callers never check consent; the storage interface and `whenGranted` do. Nobody remembers to bump a version; the lock file derives it.
- **Two categories only:** `necessary` and `analytics`. Saving a user's script, settings and dismissed hints is strictly necessary for a feature they asked for. Add a category only when a real key needs one; every category is another banner toggle.
- **Opt-in for everyone.** A static site can't reliably tell where a visitor is, so the banner is shown to everyone and no per-jurisdiction logic exists.
- **Git is the audit trail.** The registry, lock file, banner copy and scan reports are committed, so the state at any past date can be reconstructed.

## Order

- 01 → 02 → 03
- 02 → 04 → 05 and 06
- 01 → 07 → 08
- 09 needs 06 and 07; 10 needs 08
- 11 needs only 01; 13 can start any time
- 12 needs 04–06
- 14 is last

Not legal advice: have the policy text (#09, #10) reviewed before relying on it.

## Outcome

All child tickets are done. Google Analytics runs in production behind consent (#14), and the privacy scan checks every deploy against a separate GA test property (#16). Privacy for sign-in and payments continues in #15.

title: 01 · Privacy registry
description:
# 01 · Privacy registry

**Depends on:** —
**Part of:** #00

## Why

Every fact about what the site stores on a visitor's device, and which third parties it talks to, needs to live in exactly one place. The storage interface, policy page, CSP, consent purge and scans all read from it.

## What

`src/lib/privacy/registry.ts` is already drafted (site-level, not inside the teleprompter, since more Story Station tools are coming). Read it first. This ticket is to review it, test it, and remove the analytics keys that no longer need to exist.

### Design decisions already made in the draft

Keep these unless you find a concrete problem; if you do, raise it rather than working around it.

- **Plain data, typed with `as const satisfies`.** Literal keys survive (so `FirstPartyKey` and `ConsentCategoryId` can be derived) while every entry is still shape-checked.
- **No imports and only erasable TypeScript.** Node 22 can load the file directly (`node scripts/....ts`), which #07's `privacy:lock` script relies on. Don't add enums, namespaces or imports.
- **First-party entries can't be cookies.** `FirstPartyStorage["area"]` is `local | session`. The site sets no first-party cookies, so #02 doesn't need a cookie writer. Vendor entries can be any area.
- **Every storage entry has its own `category`**, even vendor-set ones, so consumers can group and purge without looking up the vendor. A test keeps it equal to the vendor's category.
- **Vendor origins are split** into `scripts` (where code loads from → CSP `script-src`) and `data` (where it sends requests → `connect-src` and `img-src`). Both use CSP host-source syntax (`https://*.example.com`). The GA values follow Google's GA4 CSP guidance; #11 re-checks them.
- **Retention is structured**, not free text: `"until-tab-closed" | "until-cleared" | { months }`. #07 needs to tell when retention gets longer (ordering: tab-closed < any months < until-cleared), and #09 renders it with `describeRetention()`.
- **Patterns.** A vendor-set name may end in `*` (`_ga_*` matches `_ga_ABC123`). `findStorageEntry(area, actualName)` is the only place that interprets that syntax; #02's purge and #12's scan both go through it rather than matching names themselves.
- **GitHub Pages is a vendor** (category `necessary`, no origins because it's `'self'`), so the privacy policy (#10) and vendor records (#13) can generate the hosting disclosure from `VENDORS`. Its `role: "controller"` reflects that GitHub logs visitor IPs for its own security purposes; #13 confirms that against GitHub's current terms.

### Remove the analytics-only keys

`tp:sessionId`, `tp:lastVisit` and `tp:visitRecorded` aren't registered and should be deleted rather than registered. Nothing user-facing depends on them, and any analytics provider we'd use (GA4 included) tracks sessions and returning visitors itself. They were also written before consent.

In `src/tools/teleprompter/lib/analytics/`:

- Remove `getSessionId()`, the module-level `sessionId`, and `session_id` from `SessionContext` (leaving `device_type`).
- Remove `recordVisit()`, the `tp_return_visit` event from `TpEvents`, and the call in `trackPageView()`.
- Update `analytics.test.ts`: delete the `recordVisit` suite and the session-id tests and assertions, and drop the `sessionStorage` stub if nothing needs it.
- Remove `lastVisit`, `sessionId` and `visitRecorded` from `KEYS` in `lib/storage.ts`. Leave the rest of that file alone; #02 replaces it.

### Classification

| Key | Area | Category | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tp:script` | local | necessary | Registered |
| `tp:settings:v1` | local | necessary | Registered |
| `tp:hintSeen` | local | necessary | Registered |
| `privacy:consent` | local | necessary | Registered now; written by #04 |
| `_ga` | cookie | analytics | Registered (Google Analytics) |
| `_ga_*` | cookie | analytics | Registered (Google Analytics) |
| `tp:sessionId`, `tp:lastVisit`, `tp:visitRecorded` | — | — | Deleted (see above) |
| `sandbox-theme` | local | — | Dev-only sandbox page, never deployed; excluded (see #03) |

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `src/lib/privacy/registry.ts` exports `CATEGORIES`, `VENDORS`, `STORAGE`, `FirstPartyKey`, `ConsentCategoryId`, `findStorageEntry` and `describeRetention` (as drafted, adjusted only with a reason).
- [ ] `tp:sessionId`, `tp:lastVisit`, `tp:visitRecorded`, `session_id` and `tp_return_visit` are gone from the code and tests.
- [ ] `src/lib/privacy/registry.test.ts` asserts:
  - every vendor-set entry names a registered vendor and has the same category as that vendor
  - no first-party name contains `*`, and only vendor-set names do
  - `purposeId` is a kebab-case slug, and each `purposeId` is used by only one entry
  - `findStorageEntry`: exact match, `_ga_*` matches `_ga_XYZ` but not `_ga` or `_gax`, the wrong area returns `undefined`, an unknown name returns `undefined`
  - `describeRetention` for each variant, including singular and plural (1 month, 13 months, 1 year, 2 years)
- [ ] A type-level check (`registry.typecheck.ts` using `// @ts-expect-error`; not `*.test.ts`, because vitest fails a file that contains no tests) shows that `"_ga"` and unregistered names aren't assignable to `FirstPartyKey`, and `"necessary"` isn't assignable to `ConsentCategoryId`. Add `"typecheck": "tsc --noEmit"` to `package.json` so it can be run. It passes today.
- [ ] `npm test` and `npm run typecheck` pass.
- [ ] Purpose, label and description text reads well on a public policy page: plain language, no internal jargon. Edit the drafted copy freely; keep `purposeId`s stable.

title: 02 · Consent-aware storage interface
description:
# 02 · Consent-aware storage interface

**Depends on:** #01
**Part of:** #00

## Why

Callers shouldn't decide where a value is stored or whether they're allowed to store it. If the interface knows a key's storage area and category from the registry, a write without consent becomes a no-op, and no caller can forget to check.

## What

Move `src/tools/teleprompter/lib/storage.ts` to `src/lib/privacy/storage.ts` and change its interface from "key + area" to "registered key":

```ts
const settings = stored("tp:settings:v1");   // key typed against the registry
settings.read();          // string | null
settings.readJSON();      // unknown
settings.write(value);    // no-op if the key's category isn't granted
settings.writeJSON(value);
settings.remove();
```

- The storage area comes from the registry; callers never pass it. First-party entries can only be `local` or `session` (#01), so `stored()` never writes cookies.
- Writes and reads for a category that isn't granted do nothing and return `null`. In dev, log a warning naming the key and category.
- Keep the existing behaviour of swallowing errors when storage is blocked (private mode, disabled storage).
- Consent is read from the consent module (#04). Until #04 lands, stub it as "analytics not granted", which is also the correct behaviour before any choice is made.
- Expose `purgeCategory(category)` that removes every registered key in that category from every area, including vendor cookies. Enumerate the names actually present in each area (localStorage, sessionStorage, `document.cookie`) and remove those where `findStorageEntry(area, name)?.category === category`. Don't match `_ga_*`-style patterns yourself. Cookies have to be deleted with the domain and path they were set with: try both host-only and `.seconddrafts.com`, path `/`.
- Delete `KEYS` from the teleprompter; callers import keys by name from the registry type.

### Migrate callers

- `src/tools/teleprompter/main.ts` (script, settings)
- `src/tools/teleprompter/prompt-hint.ts` (hintSeen)
The analytics keys (`tp:sessionId`, `tp:lastVisit`, `tp:visitRecorded`) were deleted in #01, so analytics has no storage callers to migrate.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `src/lib/privacy/storage.ts` exists; the teleprompter's `lib/storage.ts` and `KEYS` are gone.
- [ ] Passing an unregistered key is a type error.
- [ ] Unit tests: necessary keys read and write with no consent; analytics keys are no-ops without consent and work with it (no first-party analytics key exists after #01, so test with a stubbed registry entry); `purgeCategory("analytics")` removes local, session and cookie entries including `_ga_*` patterns.
- [ ] Existing teleprompter tests still pass.
- [ ] Manual check: fresh visit to the teleprompter writes only `tp:*` necessary keys.

title: 03 · Lint against direct storage access
description:
# 03 · Lint against direct storage access

**Depends on:** #02 (so the codebase passes when the rule turns on)
**Part of:** #00

## Why

The storage interface only protects us if nothing bypasses it. A lint rule catches first-party bypasses in the editor and before deploy. (It can't see aliasing tricks or third-party scripts; the scan in #12 catches those.)

## What

Add oxlint (not yet a dependency) with a `lint` script and an `.oxlintrc.json`. These built-in rules were tested on oxlint 1.87 and catch every case below without a plugin:

```json
{
  "rules": {
    "no-restricted-globals": ["error",
      { "name": "localStorage",   "message": "Use stored() from src/lib/privacy/storage." },
      { "name": "sessionStorage", "message": "Use stored() from src/lib/privacy/storage." },
      { "name": "indexedDB",      "message": "Register the store in src/lib/privacy/registry first." },
      { "name": "caches",         "message": "Register the store in src/lib/privacy/registry first." },
      { "name": "cookieStore",    "message": "Use stored() from src/lib/privacy/storage." }
    ],
    "no-restricted-properties": ["error",
      { "object": "document",   "property": "cookie" },
      { "object": "window",     "property": "localStorage" },
      { "object": "window",     "property": "sessionStorage" },
      { "object": "window",     "property": "indexedDB" },
      { "object": "globalThis", "property": "localStorage" },
      { "object": "globalThis", "property": "sessionStorage" }
    ]
  },
  "overrides": [
    { "files": ["src/lib/privacy/**"], "rules": { "no-restricted-globals": "off", "no-restricted-properties": "off" } },
    { "files": ["src/pages/sandbox/**"], "rules": { "no-restricted-globals": "off" } }
  ]
}
```

- The sandbox override is deliberate: sandbox pages are removed from the build (`astro.config.mjs`) and its `is:inline` theme script can't import modules. If sandbox pages ever ship, remove the override and register `sandbox-theme`.
- Check that oxlint lints `<script>` blocks inside `.astro` files. If it doesn't, find another way to cover them before closing this ticket.
- Add `npm run lint` to `predeploy`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `oxlint` is a dev dependency; `npm run lint` passes on the current codebase.
- [ ] A deliberate `localStorage.setItem` in a `.ts` file outside `src/lib/privacy/` fails lint.
- [ ] A deliberate `document.cookie` write inside an `.astro` `<script>` fails lint (or there's a documented alternative check).
- [ ] `predeploy` runs lint before the build.

title: 04 · Consent state
description:
# 04 · Consent state

**Depends on:** #01, #02
**Part of:** #00

## Why

The storage interface, the analytics gate and the banner all need one answer to "what has this visitor agreed to?", plus a way to react when it changes. With no server, the record of that answer also lives on the device.

## What

Create `src/lib/privacy/consent.ts`:

```ts
consent.get(category): boolean                 // necessary is always true
consent.decided(): boolean                     // a current, unexpired decision exists
consent.set(choices, source)                   // from the banner or settings
consent.onChange(listener)
consent.whenGranted(category, run)             // runs now if granted, else once it's granted
```

### The consent record

Stored under the `privacy:consent` key (necessary, localStorage) through the #02 interface:

```ts
{
  id: string,                          // random UUID, so a record can be referred to
  registryVersion: string,             // major version from the lock file (#07)
  choices: Record<ConsentCategoryId, boolean>,   // from #01; { analytics: boolean } today
  decidedAt: string,                   // ISO timestamp
  source: "banner" | "settings" | "gpc",
}
```

- **Expiry and re-prompting.** A record counts as undecided when its `registryVersion` major is older than the current one, or when it's older than `CONSENT_MAX_AGE` (6 months, CNIL's recommendation). Rejections are remembered the same way, so we don't nag.
- **GPC.** If `navigator.globalPrivacyControl === true` and there's no record, treat analytics as denied and don't show the banner (the visitor has already said no). Settings still lets them opt in explicitly, which is stored with `source: "settings"`.
- **Withdrawal.** When analytics changes from granted to denied: call `purgeCategory("analytics")` (#02), then reload the page, because a loaded `gtag.js` can't be unloaded.
- **Proof of consent.** Wrap persistence in a `recordConsent(record)` function. Today it only writes to the device. Git history of the registry, lock file and banner copy shows what the visitor was told for each `registryVersion`. If we ever add a server, a server-side log replaces `recordConsent` with no changes to callers.
- Replace the "analytics not granted" stub from #02 with this module.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `consent.ts` with the interface above and unit tests for: no record, accept, reject, expired record, older registry major, GPC with no record, GPC then explicit opt-in, withdrawal purges and reloads.
- [ ] `whenGranted` runs immediately when already granted and exactly once when granted later.
- [ ] `CONSENT_MAX_AGE` is a named constant.
- [ ] The storage interface (#02) reads consent from this module.

## Open questions

- Until #07 lands there's no lock file to read `registryVersion` from. Hard-code `"1"` and replace it in #07.

title: 05 · Gate analytics on consent
description:
# 05 · Gate analytics on consent

**Depends on:** #04
**Part of:** #00

## Why

Today `initAnalytics()` starts every configured provider on page load, which would load `gtag.js` (and set `_ga` cookies) before anyone has agreed. Analytics must start only once the analytics category is granted.

## What

In `src/tools/teleprompter/lib/analytics/index.ts` (or wherever analytics moves to when it becomes site-wide):

- `initAnalytics()` starts providers inside `consent.whenGranted("analytics", ...)`. Nothing loads before consent.
- Use the "basic" approach: don't load `gtag.js` at all until consent. Don't use Google Consent Mode's "advanced" mode, which sends cookieless pings before consent; that is legally contested in the EU and the registry/policy don't describe it.
- **Events before a decision:** keep the existing in-memory queue (it never touches device storage or the network). Flush it when analytics is granted; clear it when analytics is denied or GPC applies. This keeps the first visit's page view if the visitor accepts on that page.
- Each provider in `providers/` declares the vendor it uses (`gtag` → `google-analytics`, `console` → none) so the registry and providers can't disagree. Add a test that every non-console provider names a registered vendor.
- Keep `sanitize()` and the "no script text in events" rule as they are.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] With no consent decision, no request goes to any Google origin and no `_ga*` cookie is set (verify manually now; #12 makes it automatic).
- [ ] Accepting on the page loads the provider and sends the queued page view.
- [ ] Rejecting clears the queue and nothing is sent.
- [ ] Withdrawing later purges analytics storage and reloads (via #04).
- [ ] Unit tests cover the queue flush and clear paths.

title: 06 · Consent banner, settings and footer link
description:
# 06 · Consent banner, settings and footer link

**Depends on:** #04
**Part of:** #00

## Why

Visitors need a way to give, refuse and later change consent. Regulators (EDPB, CNIL, ICO) are specific about what a valid banner looks like, so the requirements below are not just style choices.

## What

### Banner

- Shown when `consent.decided()` is false (and GPC isn't set, see #04).
- **Accept** and **Reject** with equal visual weight, on the first layer. No "reject" hidden behind settings.
- A **Settings** option that opens the settings dialog, and a link to the cookie policy (#09).
- Nothing pre-ticked. No cookie wall: the site works fully without a choice.
- Non-modal and out of the way (for example a bottom region). Don't trap focus; give it a labelled landmark so screen readers can find it.
- **Don't overlay the teleprompter while it's prompting.** Delay the banner until the visitor leaves the prompt view. Since nothing is collected before a decision, waiting is safe.
- Copy is short and plain: what analytics is for, that it uses Google Analytics, and that rejecting changes nothing about how the tools work.
  - **Revised after release:** the banner names the purpose ("analytics") rather than the vendor, and says it never sees "what you write" rather than "your scripts", so the copy holds as vendors and tools change. Google Analytics is still named one click away, in the settings dialog and both policies.

### Settings dialog

- One toggle per consent-requiring category (only analytics today), generated from `CATEGORIES` in the registry, with each category's description.
- Shows the vendors in each category from `VENDORS`.
- Save writes through `consent.set(..., "settings")`.

### Persistent entry point

- `Base.astro` has no footer yet. Add one (or another persistent spot) with a **Cookie settings** link and links to the cookie and privacy policies.
- The cookie policy page (#09) also has a "Change your cookie settings" button.

### Design

Build with the design system (`DESIGN.md`, `design-system/`) and review it with the impeccable skill. Commit the banner copy as code, so git history shows what visitors were told for each `registryVersion` (#04).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Banner appears on a first visit and not after a decision; reappears after expiry or a registry major bump.
- [ ] Accept and Reject are the same size and weight on the first layer.
- [ ] Keyboard-only and screen-reader walkthrough passes; respects reduced motion.
- [ ] Banner never covers the prompt stage while prompting.
- [ ] Footer has Cookie settings, Cookie policy and Privacy policy links on every page.
- [ ] Settings toggles are generated from the registry, not hard-coded.

title: 07 · Registry lock file and derived version
description:
# 07 · Registry lock file and derived version

**Depends on:** #01
**Part of:** #00

## Why

A hand-bumped version depends on someone remembering to bump it. Instead, commit a snapshot of everything we disclose and fail tests when the registry drifts from it. Updating the snapshot becomes the explicit "I've checked the policy" step, and the size of the version bump is derived from what changed.

## What

- `src/lib/privacy/registry.lock.json`, committed. It holds:
  - `version` (semver), `updated` (date)
  - The disclosure fields of every category, vendor and storage entry: category, vendor, area, `purposeId`, purpose, retention, origins, transfer.
  - Not internal-only fields like `owner`.
- "Longer retention" compares the structured `Retention` values from #01: `"until-tab-closed"` < any `{ months }` (compared by number) < `"until-cleared"`.
- The registry has no imports and uses only erasable TypeScript, so the lock script can be a `.ts` file run by Node 22 directly. It currently prints a `MODULE_TYPELESS_PACKAGE_JSON` warning because `package.json` has no `"type"`. Either name the script `.mts` or check whether the existing `scripts/*.js` survive `"type": "module"`.
- `npm run privacy:lock` regenerates the lock from the registry, prints a diff, proposes the bump and writes it. The person running it can raise the bump but not lower it.
- A unit test fails when the registry and lock disagree, with a message saying to run `npm run privacy:lock` and review the cookie policy.

### Bump rules

| Bump | When | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **Major** | A category that requires consent is added, or an existing one starts requiring it. In a consent-requiring category: a controller is added or moved in, or a vendor's role changes to controller; a storage key is added, moved in or edited and either its `purposeId` had no key in that category in the previous lock, or its retention is longer than the longest the previous lock held for that `purposeId` in that category | Visitors are asked again (#04) and the policy changes |
| **Minor** | Any other disclosed change: necessary keys added or removed, processors added or swapped, a key moved into a consent category for a purpose it already had there for no longer than before, purpose wording edited, shorter retention, origins changed | Policy table and "Last updated" change |
| **Patch** | Lock metadata only | Nothing visible |

**Revised after release:** visitors consent to purposes, not to particular vendors or keys. A new or swapped processor is minor. A storage key that is new, moved into a consent-requiring category or edited is minor when the previous lock already had a key with the same `purposeId` in that category and its retention is no longer than the longest one recorded there for that `purposeId`; otherwise it is major. Swapping one analytics processor for another with the same purposes no longer re-asks everyone. Because the lock now trusts `purposeId` and `role`, `npm run privacy:lock` asks Jev whether a reworded purpose is really a new use, records each review outcome in the lock and asks a person to confirm vendor role changes; the privacy reviewer agent (`.claude/agents/privacy-reviewer.md`) checks roles, and `scripts/privacy-records-check.ts` fails while a processor in a consent-requiring category has unticked terms or data-sharing items in its `privacy/` records.

- The consent module (#04) reads the major version from the lock instead of the hard-coded `"1"`.
- The policy page (#09) reads `updated` for "Last updated".

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Lock file committed, generated from the registry including Google Analytics.
- [ ] Test fails on any registry change until the lock is regenerated.
- [ ] Unit tests for the bump rules: each row in the table above, and a combination picks the largest bump.
- [ ] #04 uses the lock's major version.

title: 08 · Treat the analytics event schema as a disclosure
description:
# 08 · Treat the analytics event schema as a disclosure

**Depends on:** #07
**Part of:** #00

## Why

What we send to an analytics provider is part of what we disclose, not just which cookies it sets. `TpEvents` in `lib/analytics/events.ts` already defines every event and property, and `sanitize()` enforces limits. But those are TypeScript types, so nothing can check them at runtime or include them in the lock file.

## What

- Turn the event definitions into a runtime schema object (event name → property names and allowed kinds), and derive the `TpEvents` types from it so the two can't disagree.
- Include event names and property names in `registry.lock.json` (#07).
- Bump rules: a new event or property is **minor** (the privacy policy's description of analytics may need checking). A property that could carry user content is never allowed (keep the existing rule in `events.ts`).
- Optionally, `sanitize()` drops properties that aren't in the schema, instead of just checking types.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Event schema exists at runtime; `TpEvents` is derived from it; existing analytics tests pass.
- [ ] Adding an event or property fails the lock test until `npm run privacy:lock` is run.
- [ ] The privacy policy (#10) describes analytics events at the level of detail the schema supports (for example "which tool settings you use, rough script length in word-count ranges, never script text").

title: 09 · Cookie policy page
description:
# 09 · Cookie policy page

**Depends on:** #01, #06, #07 (and #12 for the share-link claim)
**Part of:** #00

## Why

The draft policy (Cookie_Policy.docx, not in the repo) is a generic template. It mentions sign-in and purchases, which the site doesn't have, and lists `_gid`, which is from the old Universal Analytics, not GA4. The cookie table is the part most likely to drift, so it should be generated.

## What

Create `src/pages/cookie-policy.astro`. Write the prose by hand; generate the rest from the registry and lock file.

### Rewrite from the draft

- Company name ("The Department of Second Drafts" or the legal entity, see open questions), domain `seconddrafts.com`, contact email.
- "Cookies **and similar technologies**": explain that we mainly use local storage and session storage, which are covered the same way.
- **Strictly necessary:** saving your script, settings and dismissed hints, and remembering your consent choice. Remove sign-in and purchase.
- **Analytics:** Google Analytics. Not loaded at all until you consent. Name the data it collects, that it's shared with Google, and the international transfer basis.
- Keep: no advertising or cross-site tracking; your choices; browser controls; GPC; Google's opt-out add-on; changes; contact.
- **Your script stays on your device.** Say that the script is kept in your browser, and that share links carry the script in the part of the URL after `#`, which browsers don't send to servers. Publish this claim only once #12 proves no outgoing request contains script text.

### Generated parts

title: 11 · Content Security Policy generated from the registry
description:
# 11 · Content Security Policy generated from the registry

**Depends on:** #01
**Part of:** #00

## Why

A CSP makes the browser refuse to contact any origin we haven't listed. Generated from `VENDORS`, it means an embed or script added by accident can't reach an unregistered third party, even if every other check misses it. That protects against unregistered data transfers (visitor IPs), not just cookies.

## What

- GitHub Pages can't set response headers, so use a `<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy">` tag.
- **Use Astro's built-in support.** Astro 7 has `security.csp` in `astro.config.mjs`. It emits the meta tag, hashes Astro's own scripts and styles, and accepts extra `directives` and `scriptDirective.resources`. Build those from the registry:
  - `default-src 'self'`
  - `script-src`: `'self'` + Astro's hashes + every vendor's `origins.scripts`
  - `connect-src` and `img-src`: `'self'` + every vendor's `origins.data`
  - `font-src 'self'` (fonts are self-hosted)
- Check the GA origins against Google's own CSP guide for GA4 when implementing; Google changes them occasionally.
- Vendor origins can be included unconditionally. Consent gating is #05's job; the CSP only limits *which* third parties are reachable.
- Meta-tag CSP can't use `frame-ancestors` or `report-uri`. That's acceptable.
- CSP isn't supported in `astro dev`; test with `build` + `preview`.
- Watch for `is:inline` scripts and inline styles: both need hashes or will be blocked. The sandbox's inline script doesn't matter, since sandbox pages aren't built.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `astro.config.mjs` builds its CSP from `VENDORS` origins; no origin is written by hand.
- [ ] Built pages have the meta tag and work with no CSP errors in the console (home, blog, tools, teleprompter, cookie and privacy pages).
- [ ] A test page that loads a script from an unregistered origin is blocked.
- [ ] With analytics accepted and a test GA ID (#12), GA works with no CSP errors.

title: 12 · Privacy scan before every deploy
description:
# 12 · Privacy scan before every deploy

**Depends on:** #04, #05, #06 (#11 optional)
**Part of:** #00

## Why

Lint only sees our code. The scan is the ground truth: it loads the built site in a real browser and records everything it actually stores and contacts, including third parties and dependencies. This is the part paid consent tools charge for.

## What

`npm run privacy:scan`: a Playwright script against `astro preview` of the production build. (Chromium and Playwright are standard; add `@playwright/test` or `playwright` as a dev dependency.)

### Pages

Every URL in the built sitemap, plus the teleprompter opened with a share link.

### States

1. **No decision** (fresh context)
2. **Rejected** (via the banner)
3. **Accepted** (via the banner)
4. **GPC on** (`Sec-GPC` header and `navigator.globalPrivacyControl = true` via an init script)
5. **Accepted, then withdrawn** (via settings)

### In each state, collect

- Cookies (`context.cookies()`), localStorage and sessionStorage keys, IndexedDB database names, Cache Storage names
- The origin of every network request

### Fail the scan if

- Any key or cookie isn't in the registry. Look each one up with `findStorageEntry(area, name)` from #01, which handles patterns like `_ga_*`.
- A key in a consent-requiring category exists in a state where that category isn't granted (states 1, 2, 4, and 5 after withdrawal).
- A request goes to an origin that isn't `'self'` or a registered vendor origin, or to a consent-requiring vendor in a state without consent.

### Share-link leak check

Open the teleprompter with a share link whose script contains a unique sentinel string. Exercise it (play, change settings, accept analytics). Fail if any outgoing request URL or body contains the sentinel or its lz-string-compressed form. This proves the claim in #09 and #10.

### Testing Google Analytics for real

Use a **separate test GA property** (its own measurement ID) in the scan's build, so the accepted state sees GA's real cookies without polluting production data. Until GA is set up (#14), the accepted state just confirms no provider loads without a measurement ID.

### Record keeping

Write a report (`privacy/scan-report.json`: per state, the keys and origins seen) and commit it with each deploy. Git history then shows what the live site did at every release.

### Wire into deploy

`predeploy` becomes: lint → test → build → privacy scan.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `npm run privacy:scan` runs all five states across the sitemap and passes on the current site.
- [ ] Adding an unregistered `localStorage` key (bypassing lint), or loading a script from a new origin, fails the scan.
- [ ] The share-link sentinel check passes.
- [ ] `predeploy` runs the scan; a failing scan blocks `npm run deploy`.
- [ ] Scan report is written and committed.

title: 13 · Vendor and processing records
description:
# 13 · Vendor and processing records

**Depends on:** —
**Part of:** #00

## Why

Some obligations don't live in code: processor agreements, vendor settings, and a record of processing activities (GDPR Art. 30). The small-company exemption is unlikely to apply because analytics runs all the time, not occasionally. With two people, these need to be in the repo where they'll be seen, with dates that show when they go stale.

## What

Create a root `privacy/` folder (it will also hold the scan report from #12):

- **`privacy/vendors.md`:** one section per vendor (Google Analytics, GitHub Pages; later the email provider). Confirm the `role` and `transfer` that #01 drafted for each vendor in `VENDORS` against the vendor's current terms, especially GitHub Pages' `controller` role, and fix the registry if they're wrong. For each: what it does for us, data involved, role (processor or controller), contract or terms accepted and when, transfer mechanism, link to their privacy terms, **last reviewed** date.
- **`privacy/google-analytics.md`:** the GA property configuration checklist, to complete in #14:
  - Accept Google's data processing terms in the GA account settings
  - Data retention set to the shortest that works (GA4 offers 2 or 14 months)
  - Google Signals off
  - Granular location and device data collection off, at least for the EEA and UK
  - No links to Google Ads or other Google products
  - No user-provided data collection
  - Separate test property for the scan (#12)
- **`privacy/processing-record.md`:** the Art. 30 record, one entry per processing activity (hosting logs, analytics, later email signups). Each entry has purpose, data categories, data subjects, recipients, transfers, retention, security measures and legal basis. Generate the vendor and retention parts from the registry if that turns out to be easy; otherwise keep it short and reviewed.
- **Review cadence:** a quarterly review of these three files, the vendors' current terms, and the DPF status. Set up a recurring reminder (for example a scheduled task) and record each review by updating the "last reviewed" dates in a commit.

description:

title: 15 · Privacy changes for sign-in and payments
description:
# 15 · Privacy changes for sign-in and payments

**Depends on:** the sign-in and payments feature work (not yet ticketed)
**Part of:** — (follow-on to #00)

## Why

The privacy and cookie policies currently say there are no accounts, no payments and no email addresses collected, and that is true. Those statements must change in the same release as the features, not before: a policy has to describe what actually happens. The early draft policy had account, payment and licence sections written for this; the points below preserve them.

## What

Do all of this in the release that ships sign-in or payments, not in a later one.

- **Registry (#01):** add Stripe to `VENDORS` (a processor for payments; confirm its role, and the transfer mechanism, against its current terms). Add any email or auth provider the same way. Register every new cookie, local-storage and session-storage key for sign-in, and decide each one's category (a sign-in session cookie is strictly necessary).
- **Lock (#07):** run `npm run privacy:lock`. A new controller in a consent-requiring category, a new purpose, or a key moved into one is a major bump and re-asks visitors; a processor serving purposes visitors already agreed to, and necessary additions, are minor. Check the bump matches what you expect.
- **Privacy policy (`src/pages/privacy-policy.astro`):**
  - Remove "no accounts" and "no email addresses" from "What we don't do".
  - Add the categories of personal data: account and contact information (name, email), payment information (handled by Stripe; we receive confirmation and billing contact details but never full card numbers), and purchase and licence information (orders, licence issued, download history).
  - Add purposes and legal bases: providing the service and fulfilling purchases (performance of contract), billing and collection, support, and legal obligations.
  - Add a retention period for account and purchase records, which tax and accounting rules may require us to keep.
  - Add a Terms of Service link once a terms page exists, and the disclosure "to enforce our agreements, including billing and collection".
  - Re-check "Your rights" for what we can now actually look up and delete.
- **Cookie policy:** update the necessary-storage section for any sign-in or checkout storage (the table updates itself).
- **Email signup:** `EMAIL_CAPTURE_ENABLED` and `src/components/privacy/privacyPolicyModel.test.ts` guard the policy's "we collect no email addresses" line. Update both together, and #13's records.
- **Vendor and processing records (#13):** add Stripe and the auth or email provider to `privacy/vendors.md` and `privacy/processing-record.md`, with a processor agreement or accepted terms and a review date.
- **CSP and scan (#11, #12):** allow any new origins (Stripe's script and frames, for example) and re-run the scan; the registry should drive both.
- **Sign-in tripwire:** add a test, like the email one, that fails when sign-in is switched on while the policy still says there are no accounts.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Registry, lock, both policies, CSP and `privacy/` records all updated in the same release as the feature.
- [ ] Policy no longer says "no accounts", "no payments" or "no email addresses".
- [ ] Scan passes with the new vendors present.
- [ ] Reviewed by someone qualified before relying on it.

title: 16 · Separate Google Analytics test property for the scan
description:
# 16 · Separate Google Analytics test property for the scan

**Depends on:** #14
**Part of:** #00

## Why

Ticket 14 shipped with a single GA4 property (production). So the privacy scan never sends visits to it, `scripts/privacy-scan.ts` aborts GA's `/collect` requests (`isGoogleCollectRequest`). That means the scan proves the script, cookies, origins and request contents, but never that Google accepts the hits.

## What

1. Create a second GA4 property for testing, with the same settings as `privacy/google-analytics.md`.
2. Give the scan build its own measurement ID (a build override, kept out of `public-env/.env.production`), so the scan scans a build that reports to the test property.
3. Remove `isGoogleCollectRequest` and the route that aborts it, so the scan's accepted state sends real hits to the test property.
4. Confirm in the test property's Realtime report that scan visits appear and the production property sees none.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] Scan passes against the test property with collect requests allowed.
- [x] The production property receives no scan traffic.
- [x] `registry.lock.json` is unchanged.

## Outcome

Test property `G-RPVQBR9DFV` created 2026-10-12. `scripts/privacy-scan.ts` builds into `dist-privacy-scan/` with `PUBLIC_GA_MEASUREMENT_ID` overridden to the test ID, and scans that, so the deployed `dist/` keeps the production ID. The collect-request block is gone and the scan passes. GA4 drops visits from a `HeadlessChrome` user agent as bot traffic, so the scan's browser reports itself as plain `Chrome`; without that, Realtime showed nothing from the scan. With collect allowed, the scan no longer sees requests to `https://www.google.com`, which confirms they were GA's fallback for blocked hits. It stays registered, since real visitors on flaky networks can trigger the fallback.

Confirmed 2026-10-12: the scan's pages appear in the test property's Realtime report, and the scan build contains only the test ID. While debugging, one manual probe (not the scan) sent a single localhost page view to production by hitting a stray preview of `dist/` on port 4399.

title: 17 · Word counter v2 (overview)
description:
# 17 · Word counter v2 (overview)

Child tickets: 18–32.

## Goal

Turn the word counter from a bare first draft into a tool that sets itself apart, the way the teleprompter does. Most word counters only count. Ours should help with the next step, a second draft: hitting a format's limit, seeing what has to be cut, and knowing how long the piece runs aloud.

It's still a cheap bet, like the teleprompter: no backend, no accounts, and the visitor's text never leaves the browser.

## Where it stands

`src/pages/tools/word-counter.astro` is one 170-line page holding its markup, styles and script. It has no persistence, analytics or SEO content. It also has its own `countWords`, separate from the teleprompter's `lib/timing.ts`, so the two tools can disagree about the same text.

## Shared design

- **One module for measuring text** (#18). Both tools count words, characters and speaking time through it, so they always agree.
- **The tool lives in `src/tools/word-counter/`**, laid out like `src/tools/teleprompter/`: a small store, mount functions per part of the UI, and a thin `main.ts`. The page in `src/pages/tools/` only composes components.
- **One target model** (#19). A target is a unit, a number and a rule. Presets are named targets. The status line, the cut line (#27) and analytics all read from that single model, so none of them needs to know about presets.
- **Privacy rules carry over unchanged.** New storage keys go in the registry (`src/lib/privacy/registry.ts`). New events go in `EVENT_SCHEMA`, and properties never carry visitor text or anything derived from it beyond a word-count bucket. Run `npm run privacy:lock` after either change.
- **The privacy scan drives this page.** `scripts/privacy-scan.ts` (`countWords`, around line 210) clicks `#show-target`, `#unit` and `#style`. Any ticket that changes those controls updates the scan in the same commit.

## Order

The difficult, shared logic comes first and is done serially, so the later tickets are UI wiring against a stable, tested API and can run in parallel without touching the same files.

| Phase | Tickets | Model | Why this order |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 · Foundations | #18 measurement (word spans, limit offsets, sentences, speaking time) | Opus | Every count, cut and selection reads from it |
| 0 · Foundations | #19 module, target model and status, shared infra | Opus | The layout every later ticket adds to; the one target model |
| 1 · Shared registries | #20 saving, then #23 analytics | Sonnet | Both change the privacy registry and lock file, so they run one after the other |
| 2 · Features | #27 cut line | Opus | The highlight layer is the riskiest UI work |
| 2 · Features | #25 presets, #28 selection, #29 session progress, #30 rhythm | Sonnet | Independent of each other |
| 2 · Features | #21 speaking time | Haiku | Display only |
| 2 · Features | #22 open in teleprompter, #24 SEO | Sonnet | After #21 |
| Later | #26 preset landing pages | — | Once #23 shows which presets people use |
| Later | #31 writing sprint tool, spun out of #29 | — | Sprints need a focused writing screen, not a panel in the counter |
| Later | #32 writing analysis tool, spun out of #30 | — | Rhythm is one view of a bigger analysis tool, not a counter panel |

Phase 2 tickets each add one component and one mount line, and call analytics hooks #23 already registered, so they don't edit `EVENT_SCHEMA`, the lock file or the settings validator. Run each in its own worktree and merge them one at a time.

title: 18 · Shared text measurement module
description:
# 18 · Shared text measurement module

**Depends on:** none
**Part of:** #17

## Why

The word counter and the teleprompter each have their own `countWords`. Today they happen to match, but they'll drift, and a writer who pastes the same script into both should never see two different numbers. Character counts are also wrong: `text.length` counts UTF-16 code units, so 👍 counts as 2 and an accented letter typed as a base letter plus a combining mark counts as 2.

## What

Create `src/lib/text/measure.ts` (or a better name chosen during design) as the single place that measures text. Rough interface:

```ts
wordSpans(text): [start, end][]          // the primitive; everything about words derives from it
countWords(text): number                 // wordSpans(text).length
countCharacters(text): number            // user-perceived characters (Intl.Segmenter, "grapheme")
countCharactersWithoutSpaces(text): number
limitOffset(text, unit, limit): number | null   // where a limit falls; null when under it
sentences(text): { start, end, words }[]
speakingSeconds(words, wpm?): number      // moved from teleprompter readTimeSeconds
formatSpeakingTime(seconds): string       // moved from teleprompter formatReadTime
wordBucket(words): WordBucket             // moved from teleprompter lib/timing.ts
```

Word positions, limit offsets and sentences live here, not in the tickets that display them (#27 cut line, #28 selection, #30 rhythm), so every feature counts the same way.

- Move the text helpers out of `src/tools/teleprompter/lib/timing.ts`. The scroll-timing helpers (`remainingSeconds`, `formatClock`) stay where they are.
- Decide what a word is, and pin it with a table-driven test. Cases to settle:

  | Text | Notes |
  |---|---|
  | `don't` | 1 |
  | `well-known` | 1 (the usual convention in word processors) |
  | `word—word` (em dash, no spaces) | Word processors disagree. Pick one; 2 matches how people read it |
  | `3.14`, `$1,000`, `10:30` | 1 each |
  | `— ` on its own, `…`, `*` | 0, since punctuation alone isn't a word |
  | URLs and emails | 1 each |
  | `日本語の文章` | Whitespace splitting says 1. Decide whether to support CJK now with `Intl.Segmenter` word granularity (`isWordLike`) or record it as out of scope |

  Design it twice: compare whitespace-plus-dash splitting against `Intl.Segmenter("word")`. Segmenter splits `well-known` into two, so it may only be right as a CJK fallback.
- `countCharacters` falls back to `Array.from(text).length` where `Intl.Segmenter` is missing.
- **Limit offsets** (for #27). `limitOffset(text, unit, limit)` returns the UTF-16 offset of the first word or character past the limit, for `words`, `characters` and `seconds` (seconds convert to words through the speaking pace). It must agree with the counts: the text before the offset counts as exactly the limit. It must stay fast at 20,000 words.
- **Sentences** (for #30). `Intl.Segmenter("sentence")` splits `Dr. Smith went home.` after `Dr.`, so merge common abbreviations back (`Dr.`, `Mr.`, `Mrs.`, `Ms.`, `St.`, `e.g.`, `i.e.`, `etc.` followed by a lowercase word, initials). Also handle ellipses, dialogue in quotes, and line breaks without punctuation.
- **Speaking time under a minute** (decided for #21). Below 60 seconds, show seconds rounded to 5 (`About 45 sec`) in both tools, since people check 30- and 60-second scripts. Zero words show nothing.
- **Longer word buckets** (for #23). Extend `WordBucket` with `601-2000`, `2001-10000` and `10000+`, in place of `600+`, for both tools. Run `npm run privacy:lock` and check the privacy policy's analytics description still fits.
- Update the teleprompter's imports. Its displayed counts and `word_bucket` values may shift slightly for edge cases. That's expected, and the tests should say so.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] One module measures text; the teleprompter and the word counter both import from it, and neither defines its own `countWords`.
- [x] Table-driven tests cover every case above with the chosen answers.
- [x] 👍, `é` written as `e` + U+0301, and 🇺🇸 each count as one character.
- [x] Existing teleprompter tests pass (updating any expectation that the new word rules intentionally change).
- [x] `limitOffset` tests cover words, characters (including emoji and combining marks) and seconds, at, under and over the limit, and text before the offset always measures exactly the limit.
- [x] `sentences` tests cover abbreviations, ellipses, quoted dialogue and unpunctuated line breaks.
- [x] Under a minute reads in seconds in both tools.
- [x] `WordBucket` has the longer buckets, and the lock test passes.

## Outcome

`src/lib/text/measure.ts` holds words, characters, limit offsets, speaking time and word buckets. `src/lib/text/sentences.ts` holds sentence splitting. The teleprompter's `lib/timing.ts` keeps only the scroll-timing helpers.

**What a word is.** I compared the two designs. `Intl.Segmenter("word")` splits `well-known`, URLs, emails and `$1,000` into pieces, so it's wrong as the main rule. Words are the text between separators, which are:

- whitespace;
- em and en dashes and the horizontal bar;
- two or more hyphens;
- `…` or three or more dots.

A token only counts if it holds a letter or number, so `—`, `*`, `&` and an emoji alone count 0. Tokens from scripts written without spaces (Han, Hiragana, Katakana, Thai, Lao, Khmer, Myanmar) are split with `Intl.Segmenter("word")`. Its Japanese splits are dictionary-based, so CJK counts are approximate but sensible. Without `Intl.Segmenter`, such a token counts as one word.

**Sentences.** `Intl.Segmenter("sentence")` splits after `Mr.` and initials, and between `"Stop!"` and `she said`, so segments are merged back:

- when the previous one ends in a title abbreviation or a single initial;
- when the next one starts lowercase.

A line break always ends a sentence. `…` is treated like `...`, which the segmenter otherwise handles differently. Without `Intl.Segmenter`, each line is a sentence.

**Speaking time.** Below a minute it reads in seconds rounded to 5 (minimum 5) in both tools, so the teleprompter now shows `About 45 sec to read` where it said `Under a minute to read`.

**Word buckets** gained `601-2000`, `2001-10000` and `10000+`. The lock records only that `word_bucket` is a string, so the lock and its version didn't change, and the privacy policy's "ranges of word counts" still fits.

**Performance.** At 20,000 words, `limitOffset` and `sentences` take a few milliseconds. Counting graphemes takes about 30 ms, which only matters with a characters target on very long text. #27 should re-measure it with the highlight layer in place.

title: 19 · Word counter fixes, accessibility and module move
description:
# 19 · Word counter fixes, accessibility and module move

**Depends on:** #18
**Part of:** #17

## Why

The current page has several bugs that visitors will see, and it's built as one inline script, which makes every later ticket harder. Fixing the bugs is a good moment to give it the same structure as the teleprompter.

## What

### Move into a module

- Move the script out of `src/pages/tools/word-counter.astro` into `src/tools/word-counter/`, following the teleprompter's layout: a small store for `{ text, target }`, one mount function per part of the UI, and a thin `main.ts`. Use the shared `required()` from `src/lib/dom` in place of the page's own `querySelector` helper.
- Use #18 for all counting.
- Lay it out so later tickets don't collide: `main.ts` is a flat list of `mountX(store, hooks)` calls, and the page composes one `.astro` component per feature. A feature ticket (#21, #25, #27–#30) then adds one component and one mount line.

### Shared infrastructure

Several later tickets need the same teleprompter pieces. Promote them here, once, rather than in parallel tickets:

- `src/tools/teleprompter/lib/debounce.ts` moves to `src/lib/debounce.ts`.
- `confirm.ts` and `ConfirmDialog.astro` move to `src/lib/` and `src/components/`, for #20's Clear button.
- The teleprompter's store becomes a generic `createStore<State>` in `src/lib/`, and both tools use it.

### Target model (moved from #25)

A target is `{ unit, value, rule }`, with an optional `min` for ranges:

- `unit`: `words`, `characters` or `seconds` (spoken, via #18).
- `rule`: `at-most`, `at-least`, `exactly` or `around` (within a tolerance). The UI uses these plain words in place of Min, Max and Goal.

One pure function evaluates a measurement against a target and returns its state and status text. The colour, status line, cut line (#27), selection line (#28), presets (#25) and analytics (#23) all read from it. A `seconds` target's status reads in time (`15 sec to go`).

This ticket builds the model and the custom-target controls. #25 adds named presets on top.

### Bugs

- **The colour shows with the target turned off.** With "Show target" off, the count still turns red or green against a hidden target. With the target off, the count stays the normal ink colour.
- **A target of 0 or an empty target** divides by zero. An empty, zero or invalid target means "no target", which removes the special case.
- **The target only updates on `change`.** Typing a new number doesn't update the count until blur. Listen for `input`.
- **Large numbers aren't formatted.** Use `Intl.NumberFormat` for the count and target (`1,240 / 1,000 words`), like the teleprompter's edit view.
- **Wrong plural.** `1 words` should read `1 word`.

### Accessibility

- **Status is shown only by colour.** Add a text status next to the count, worded by the rule: `38 to go`, `12 over`, `On target`, `Within 5%`. Colour stays as a second cue.
- Give the status an `aria-live="polite"` region and announce changes only after typing settles (about 1 second), so screen readers aren't flooded on every keystroke.
- Keep the visible focus styles the page already has.

### Privacy scan

Update `scripts/privacy-scan.ts` for the renamed rule control.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] The page's script lives in `src/tools/word-counter/`, and the `.astro` page holds only markup, styles and component composition.
- [x] With the target off, the count is never coloured.
- [x] A target of 0, empty or negative behaves as no target; no `Infinity` or `NaN` reaches the DOM.
- [x] Typing in the target field updates the display immediately.
- [x] Each rule shows a text status; a screen reader announces the settled status once after typing stops.
- [x] Unit tests cover the status wording for each rule and unit, at, under and over target, including ranges (`min`) and `seconds`.
- [x] `debounce`, the confirm dialog and the store live in shared locations, and the teleprompter uses them.
- [x] `npm run privacy:scan` passes.

## Outcome

**Layout.** `src/tools/word-counter/`:

- `lib/state.ts`: the state is `{ text, showTarget, target }`. `activeTarget()` and `summarize()` derive the count line and evaluation from it.
- `lib/target.ts`: the target model and `evaluateTarget`.
- `lib/readout.ts`: the count text and amount formatting.
- One `.astro` component and one `mountX(store)` per part: `Editor`, `CountLine`, `TargetPanel`.
- `main.ts` is the list of mounts, and puts the store on `window.__wcStore` in dev.

**Shared infrastructure.**

- `src/lib/store.ts` is the generic `createStore(initial, apply)`, with `mergeShallow` for flat state. The teleprompter passes its nested-settings merge.
- `src/lib/debounce.ts` is shared.
- `src/lib/confirm.ts` and `src/components/ConfirmDialog.astro` are shared, using `data-confirm` and `data-confirm-part`.

**Target decisions.**

- A target is active only when it's switched on and its value is above 0. An empty or partly typed number is stored as 0, so `NaN` never reaches the store or the DOM.
- `around` allows ±10% (`AROUND_TOLERANCE`).
- `min` makes anything below it "under", whatever the rule.
- `seconds` amounts are rounded to whole seconds before evaluating, so a status never reads "0 sec to go".
- Status wording by rule:

  | Rule | Under | At | Over |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | at-most | `38 left` | `At the limit` | `12 over` |
  | at-least | `38 to go` | `Target reached` | `Target reached` |
  | exactly | `38 to go` | `On target` | `12 over` |
  | around | `38 to go` outside the tolerance, `Within 4%` inside it | `On target` | `12 over` outside the tolerance, `Within 4%` inside it |

- Colour: met is `--green-ink` and over is `--red-pen`. Under, and any count without a target, is the normal ink colour.

**The page.**

- The controls are `#wc-text`, `#wc-show-target`, `#wc-rule`, `#wc-target` and `#wc-unit`. The unit select gained "Seconds aloud". The privacy scan step is updated, and the scan passes.
- The live region announces `count, status` once typing has been still for one second, and never repeats an unchanged announcement.

title: 20 · Keep the visitor's text and settings
description:
# 20 · Keep the visitor's text and settings

**Depends on:** #19
**Part of:** #17

## Why

The text disappears on reload. People paste in drafts they care about, and losing one is the fastest way to make sure they don't come back. The teleprompter already solved this with the consent-aware storage interface (#02).

## What

- Register two first-party keys in `STORAGE` in `src/lib/privacy/registry.ts`, both `necessary`, `local`, `until-cleared`:
  - `wc:text`: "Keeps the text you're counting in your browser, so it's still there when you come back."
  - `wc:settings:v1`: "Remembers your word counter target and format."
- Read and write them through `stored()` from `src/lib/privacy/storage.ts`, debounced like the teleprompter's `persistChanges` (500 ms for text, 300 ms for settings, flushed on `pagehide`).
- Validate saved settings on read, so a stale or hand-edited value falls back to defaults instead of breaking the page. Validate field by field, so one bad field doesn't discard the rest.
- Settings hold the target (#19), the chosen preset ID or `custom` (#25), and whether the rhythm strip is open (#30). Add all three now with defaults, so #25 and #30 don't need to change the validator.
- Add a **Clear** button with a confirm step, using the shared confirm dialog #19 promoted to `src/lib/` and `src/components/`.
- Run `npm run privacy:lock`. New necessary keys are a minor bump; confirm the generated cookie policy table lists them.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] Type text, set a target, reload: both are restored.
- [x] Clear asks first, and after confirming, a reload shows an empty field.
- [x] Invalid saved settings fall back to defaults without errors.
- [x] The cookie policy lists `wc:text` and `wc:settings:v1`.
- [x] `npm run privacy:scan` passes and reports only registered keys.
- [x] No text reaches any network request (the scan already checks for this).

## Outcome

- `wc:text` and `wc:settings:v1` are registered (lock bumped to 2.1.0) and read and written through `stored()` by `src/tools/word-counter/persistence.ts`.
- `validateSettings` in `lib/settings.ts` validates field by field. Settings hold `showTarget`, `target`, `presetId` and `rhythmOpen`, all now in `State`, so #25 and #30 only read and write them.
- Clear sits under the text field and uses the shared confirm dialog.
- Checked by unit tests, `privacy:scan` and the built cookie policy page. The reload round trip wasn't exercised in a browser.

title: 21 · Show speaking time
description:
# 21 · Show speaking time

**Depends on:** #18, #19 (display only; the formatter is done in #18)
**Part of:** #17

## Why

A lot of word counting is really time counting: a two-minute talk, a 60-second ad read, a five-minute open-mic slot. The teleprompter already estimates read time at 150 words per minute. Showing it here costs almost nothing and points naturally toward the teleprompter (#22).

## What

- Next to the count, show the speaking time from #18: `412 words · About 3 min aloud`.
- Use #18's `formatSpeakingTime`, which already shows seconds under a minute (`About 45 sec aloud`). This ticket is display only; don't change the formatter.
- Say the assumed pace once, in quiet text or a tooltip: "at 150 words per minute, a relaxed speaking pace." Don't add a speed control yet.
- Hide the speaking time when the text is empty.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] The speaking time updates as the visitor types and matches the teleprompter's estimate for the same text.
- [x] Under a minute shows seconds; an hour or more shows hours and minutes.
- [x] The assumed pace is stated somewhere on the page (as a tooltip on the time).

## Outcome

- The time sits on a second line under the count, with "Open in Teleprompter" at the right of the same line, and hides when the text is empty. A first version stated the pace as a line of text; it cluttered the page, so the pace is now only the tooltip on the time ("At 150 words per minute"). Touch users don't see a tooltip, so the "stated somewhere on the page" criterion is met weakly.
- The time uses `formatSpeakingTime(speakingSeconds(words))`, the same call the teleprompter makes, via `speakingTime` in `lib/state.ts`.
- It hides when the target is in "minutes aloud", because the count already reads in spoken time and a second time would repeat it.
- It stays out of the polite live region, so screen readers aren't told on every keystroke.

title: 22 · Open the text in the teleprompter
description:
# 22 · Open the text in the teleprompter

**Depends on:** #19, #21, #23
**Part of:** #17

## Why

Someone checking the length of a script is often about to read it aloud. A one-click handoff to the teleprompter serves them and moves traffic between the two tools.

## What

- Add an **Open in Teleprompter** link near the speaking time. It's shown when there's text.
- Reuse the share-link path the teleprompter already has (`buildShareUrl` in `src/tools/teleprompter/lib/share.ts`). That gives the existing "replace your saved script?" confirm on arrival for free, and nothing new is written to storage from the word counter.
- **Don't overwrite the visitor's teleprompter settings.** Today `openShareLink` in `teleprompter/main.ts` applies the shared settings along with the script. A handoff should carry the script only, so someone's chosen font and theme survive. Make `settings` optional in `SharePayload`, and omit the `s` field from the payload when it's absent: no `s` means "keep mine". `buildShareUrl` has always written `s`, even as `{}` for default settings, so every existing link keeps applying its settings.
- Report the handoff with `tp_script_entered { source: "word_counter" }` (registered in #23), so it is told apart from shared links.
- Long text is fine: the URL never leaves the browser, so the `SHARE_URL_WARN_LENGTH` warning doesn't apply here.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] Clicking the link opens the teleprompter with the text loaded.
- [x] If the teleprompter already holds a different script, the existing confirm appears; "Keep mine" leaves it untouched.
- [x] The visitor's saved teleprompter font, theme and other settings are unchanged after a handoff.
- [x] Existing share links still open with their settings.
- [x] `tp_script_entered` fires with `source: "word_counter"` for a handoff.
- [x] Share-link tests cover the script-only payload.

## Outcome

- The link sits in the count line, since #21 (speaking time) isn't built yet. Move it beside the speaking time when that lands.
- A script-only link has no `s` field and carries `o: "word_counter"`. Opening it leaves the visitor's teleprompter settings alone. Links with `s` apply their settings as before. A link without `s` used to decode to default settings; it now decodes to none.
- A handoff gets its own confirm wording ("Open this text in the teleprompter?"), reports `tp_script_entered` with `source: "word_counter"`, and does not fire `tp_share_link_opened`.
- The link's `href` is built on hover, focus and click rather than per keystroke, so open-in-new-tab works.

title: 23 · Word counter analytics
description:
# 23 · Word counter analytics

**Depends on:** #19
**Part of:** #17

## Why

We can't tell yet whether anyone uses the word counter, or which of the bigger features (#26, #29, #30) are worth the effort. The teleprompter's events answered that question for it. Same approach, same privacy rule.

## What

Add `wc_` events to `EVENT_SCHEMA` in `src/lib/analytics/events.ts`. Properties never carry text or anything derived from it beyond a word-count bucket.

| Event | Properties | When |
|---|---|---|
| `wc_text_entered` | `word_bucket`, `source` (`paste` / `typed` / `restored`) | Once per visit, after text settles (like `tp_script_entered`) |
| `wc_target_set` | `preset` (preset ID or `custom`), `unit`, `rule` | When a target is chosen, debounced |
| `wc_target_reached` | `preset`, `rule` | First time per visit the status becomes on-target |
| `wc_opened_in_teleprompter` | `word_bucket` | #22 handoff |
| `wc_engaged` | `word_bucket`, `duration_s` | Active for more than 60 s with more than 50 words, like `tp_engaged` |

Register the later tickets' events here as well, with their hooks, so those tickets only call a hook and never edit `EVENT_SCHEMA` or the lock file. Several of them would otherwise run in parallel and conflict on both:

| Event | Properties | Fired by |
|---|---|---|
| `wc_cut_line_shown` | `rule`, `unit` | #27, once per visit |
| `wc_selection_counted` | none | #28, once per visit |
| `wc_sprint_started` | `minutes` | #29 |
| `wc_sprint_finished` | `minutes`, `word_bucket` | #29 |
| `wc_rhythm_opened` | none | #30 |
| `wc_rhythm_sentence_clicked` | none | #30 |

Also add `word_counter` to `ScriptSource` for #22's `tp_script_entered`.

- Put the tracking in `src/tools/word-counter/usage-tracking.ts`, mirroring the teleprompter's file, so the UI code only calls hooks.
- Make one `npm run privacy:lock` bump for all of it. The longer word buckets are done in #18.
- **Optional fake doors.** If you'd rather sequence #26, #29 and #30 by demand than build them all, ship them as fake doors first. Generalise `FakeDoors.astro`, `fake-doors.ts` and the `tp_fake_door_*` events so both tools share them; don't copy them.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] All events above fire with the correct properties (unit tests, like `usage-tracking.test.ts`).
- [x] Every event for #22 and #27–#30 is in the schema with a hook, so those tickets don't touch the schema or lock file.
- [x] No event fires before analytics consent.
- [x] `npm run privacy:lock` run; the lock test passes.
- [x] The privacy policy's analytics description covers the word counter.

## Outcome

- All eleven `wc_*` events are in `EVENT_SCHEMA` and the lock (2.2.0), and `ScriptSource` gains `word_counter`. Jev flagged `wc_text_entered.word_bucket` (0.42); it is the same six-value `WordBucket` as `tp_script_entered`, and the lock was confirmed.
- `src/tools/word-counter/usage-tracking.ts` fires the first five from the store. `UsageHooks` carries `onOpenedInTeleprompter`, `onCutLineShown`, `onSelectionCounted`, `onSprintStarted`, `onSprintFinished`, `onRhythmOpened` and `onRhythmSentenceClicked` for #22 and #27–#30.
- `wc_target_reached` ignores empty text and restored state, so "at most" doesn't fire trivially. `wc_engaged` counts from the first edit.
- The privacy policy lists events from the schema, so it needed no copy change.
- No fake doors: #26, #29 and #30 stay real tickets.

description:

title: 25 · Format presets
description:
# 25 · Format presets

**Depends on:** #19, #20, #23
**Part of:** #17

## Why

The Targets panel asks for a unit, a number and a rule. That's hard to fill in at a glance, and it isn't how writers think. They think in formats: a drabble, a Common App essay, a post on Bluesky. One picker that sets all three is easier to use, and it's the feature that most sets this tool apart.

## What

### Presets

The target model, its rules, ranges, `seconds` unit and status wording are built in #19. This ticket adds named presets on top and doesn't change how targets are evaluated.

- A preset is `{ id, name, group, description, target }`. Its target uses #19's model, including `min` for ranges (Common App: 250–650 words).
- Status, colour, the cut line (#27) and analytics (#23) read from the target, never from the preset.
- The saved settings already have a `preset` field (#20).

### Picker

- One select or combobox at the top of the panel: **None**, a list of presets grouped by kind, and **Custom**.
- Choosing a preset fills in the unit, value and rule, and shows a one-line description ("A story of exactly 100 words").
- Editing any field switches the picker to Custom while keeping the values.
- The chosen preset or custom target is saved via #20.

### Starting presets

Confirm every number against a current source before shipping; platform limits change.

| Group | Preset | Target |
|---|---|---|
| Fiction | Six-word story | exactly 6 words |
| Fiction | Drabble | exactly 100 words |
| Fiction | Microfiction | at most 300 words |
| Fiction | Flash fiction | at most 1,000 words |
| Fiction | Short story | at most 7,500 words |
| Submissions | Query letter | around 300 words |
| Submissions | One-page synopsis | at most 500 words |
| Submissions | Logline | at most 50 words |
| Essays | Common App personal essay | 250–650 words |
| Social | X post | at most 280 characters (note that X weights links and some scripts differently) |
| Social | Bluesky post | at most 300 characters |
| Social | Threads post | at most 500 characters |
| Spoken | 30-second read | around 30 seconds |
| Spoken | 60-second read | around 60 seconds |
| Spoken | Five-minute talk | around 5 minutes |

### Privacy scan

The scan's `countWords` step sets a custom target (updated in #19). Update it to pick a preset first.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] Choosing a preset sets unit, value and rule; editing any of them switches to Custom.
- [x] The Common App preset shows under, within and over correctly (the range logic itself is tested in #19).
- [x] The spoken presets count speaking time, and their status reads in time ("15 sec to go").
- [x] The preset survives a reload.
- [x] Every preset number has been checked against a current source, with the source noted in the ticket's Outcome.
- [x] `npm run privacy:scan` passes with the updated scan step.

## Notes from #19

The custom-target controls have no field for `min`. If someone picks a range preset (Common App) and then edits a field, the picker switches to Custom. Either show a minimum field for that case or drop `min`; don't keep a range the visitor can't see.

## Outcome

Added `lib/presets.ts` (the 15 presets, grouping and picker helpers, tested in `presets.test.ts`) and a **Format** picker at the top of the Targets panel: None, presets grouped by kind, Custom, with a one-line description under it. Choosing a preset sets the target, turns "Show target" on and saves `presetId` through the existing settings. No storage, registry, event or lock-file changes. The privacy scan now picks the Query letter preset, then switches the unit to characters so the custom-target path is still driven.

Decisions:
- **None** hides the target and keeps the values; ticking "Show target" while on None moves the picker to Custom. A saved id that is no longer in the list shows as Custom.
- **Range presets (`min`):** editing any field drops `min` and switches to Custom, since no field shows a minimum. Picking Common App, then changing 650 to 500 gives a plain "at most 500". Adding a minimum field would be a separate ticket.
- The X description mentions link and script weighting; the counter itself still counts characters.

Sources (checked 2026-10-13, via web search; official pages were not directly fetched):
- Common App 250-650 words: Common App essay guides (Solomon Admissions, Cognito 2026-27 prompts) and The Harvard Crimson on strict enforcement. Unchanged.
- Bluesky 300 characters: several tool and vendor pages agree; Bluesky counts graphemes, so emoji count as one. Unchanged.
- Threads 500 characters: OneUp and Emplifi; Threads also has 10,000-character text attachments, which this preset ignores. Sources conflict on whether links count. Unchanged.
- X 280 characters: Circleboom, Bundle.social, Metricool; links count as 23, and sources disagree on emoji weighting. Premium accounts can post longer. Unchanged.
- Drabble 100, six-word story 6, microfiction 300, flash fiction 1,000: Scribophile, Masters Review, SF Encyclopedia. Boundaries are loose conventions. Unchanged.
- Short story 7,500: SFWA Nebula rules (short story under 7,500 words). Unchanged.
- Query letter ~300: informal advice of 250-350 words (Anne R. Allen, Jericho Writers); agents' own guidelines override it. Unchanged.
- One-page synopsis 500: most sources (We Are Whitefox, others). Unchanged.
- Logline 50: sources only say one or two sentences. No source found for a 50-word figure, so it is a convention, not a verified limit.
- Spoken presets use the shared speaking-time measure; nothing external to check.

Not verified: the official X, Bluesky, Threads and Common App pages. `npm run typecheck` reports three pre-existing errors in `src/lib/blog.ts` that this change doesn't touch.
- Later redesigned after use: the Show target checkbox and the grouped Format dropdown were replaced. A "Set a target" link in the count line opens a drawer with the target as one sentence ("Aim for at most 240 words") and the formats as links underneath. No target is the default, and an empty number means none. A "between" rule shows a range's minimum, so editing Common App keeps it instead of dropping it. It was chosen from four prototypes (a fill-in sentence, a shelf of formats, a search field, and a link in the count line); the shipped design combines the first and last.
