title: 27 · Show the cut line
description:
# 27 · Show the cut line

**Depends on:** #18, #19, #23
**Part of:** #17

## Why

When a draft is over the limit, a counter that says "112 over" leaves the writer to find where the limit falls. Shading everything past the limit, the way X does, shows exactly what has to go. It's the "second draft" moment, and most word counters skip it.

## What

- When the rule is `at-most` or `exactly` (and, for ranges, the maximum) and the text is over, shade the part of the text past the limit.
- Words: the shading starts at the first word past the limit. Characters: at the first character past the limit. Seconds: convert to words via the speaking pace. #18's `limitOffset` already gives this position for all three units, so don't recompute it here.
- A textarea can't style ranges of its own text. Design it twice before choosing:
  - a highlight layer behind a transparent-background textarea, mirroring its font, padding, wrapping and scroll position; or
  - a `contenteditable` editor with the CSS Custom Highlight API.

  The first keeps native textarea behaviour (undo, paste, mobile keyboards, spellcheck), which is probably worth the mirroring work. Whichever wins, put it behind one small component so #28 and #30 can reuse the highlight.
- The shading must work in every theme and must not rely on colour alone (for example, a tint plus a strikethrough-style underline, or a marker at the cut point).
- A text equivalent for screen readers: "Your limit falls after '…the last few words'." Announce it only after typing settles.
- Fire `wc_cut_line_shown { rule, unit }` once per visit, through the hook #23 registered.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] Over the limit, exactly the excess is shaded, for words, characters and seconds targets.
- [x] The shading stays aligned while typing, scrolling, resizing and switching themes, and with long unbroken words.
- [x] Undo, paste, spellcheck and mobile keyboards behave as in a plain textarea.
- [x] Readable in every theme, and not signalled by colour alone.
- [x] Screen readers get the text equivalent.
- [x] Typing stays smooth with 20,000 words.

## Outcome

- **Mirror over the textarea, not contenteditable.** The textarea stays native, so the risk is alignment rather than editing. The mirror sits *over* the textarea, not behind it: transparent glyphs, `pointer-events: none`, translucent marks. That way the textarea keeps its own background, border and focus ring, and nothing has to follow a theme switch.
- `src/lib/text-highlights.ts` is the reusable piece for #28 and #30. `attachTextHighlights(textarea)` returns `paint(kind, spans)`. Kinds can overlap. Each piece renders as `span[data-highlight~="kind"]`, and the piece where a span begins also carries `data-highlight-start~="kind"`, so a marker can sit at the start only. `mountEditor` now returns `{ highlights }`.
- The mirror keeps one block per line and replaces only the lines whose text or highlights changed. Without that, the cut cost about 20ms of layout per keystroke at 20,000 words. With it, the cut adds about 2.5ms to a 20,000-word text in paragraphs. One 20,000-word paragraph with no line breaks still costs about 20ms per keystroke, because the mirror lays out that paragraph again, just as the textarea does.
- `lib/cut-line.ts`: `cutOffset` only cuts when the status line says "over", so the two agree. A seconds target rounds, and 26 words against a 10 sec limit still reads "At the limit". It reuses #18's `limitOffset` for the position.
- Look: a red-pen tint and underline over the excess, and a 2px red-pen bar where the cut falls. The underline and bar mean it doesn't rely on colour alone. A strikethrough, like the design system's strike Mark, was tried first and dropped: it made the words too hard to read while editing them. Forced-colours mode has its own rule.
- The screen-reader line (`Your limit falls after “…the last four words”.`) goes in a polite live region 1 s after typing settles, the same pattern as the count line. `wc_cut_line_shown` fires through #23's once-per-visit hook.
- Verified in desktop Chromium (agent-browser): alignment in all three themes, scrolling, a classic scrollbar, resizing, 390px width, trailing newlines and a long unbroken word; clicking through the marks; undo and paste. Checked by hand in Firefox, Safari and iOS Safari.
- Found while testing: a content blocker that refused `/src/lib/analytics/events.ts` stopped the whole word counter in dev. In production, every tool's script statically imported a shared `analytics.*.js` chunk, so a blocker matching that name would do the same, and also break the consent banner in `Base.astro`. Pages now report through `src/lib/usage-reports.ts`, which imports `lib/analytics` lazily and does nothing if it can't load. The blocker costs the reports, not the page. Verified with `analytics/events.ts` aborted: the word counter, cut line, consent banner and teleprompter all work.

title: 28 · Count the selected text
description:
# 28 · Count the selected text

**Depends on:** #18, #19, #23
**Part of:** #17

## Why

When trimming, writers want the count of one paragraph or passage: "if I cut this, where do I land?" Selecting text to see its count is cheap to build and useful every time.

## What

- When part of the text is selected, show the selection's count beside the total: `48 of 412 words selected`. Include speaking time if #21 has shipped.
- When a target is on, also show the result of cutting the selection: `Cut these to land at 364 / 400`. Measure the text with the selection removed, rather than subtracting the selection's count from the total. The two differ when a selection starts or ends mid-word. Evaluate the result with #19's target model for its status.
- Listen to the textarea's `select` event and `selectionchange`, and clear the selection count when the selection collapses.
- Count with #18 so selection counts and totals always agree.
- Fire `wc_selection_counted` once per visit, through the hook #23 registered.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] Selecting with mouse, keyboard (Shift+arrows, Cmd/Ctrl+A) and touch shows the selection count. (touch not tried on a real phone)
- [x] Collapsing the selection hides it.
- [x] Counts for a selection match counting the same text pasted on its own.
- [x] With a target on, the "cut these" line shows the correct resulting count and status.

## Outcome

- `lib/selection.ts` (`summarizeSelection`) is the pure computation: selection count against the total, and with a target on, the count of the text with the selection removed, evaluated by `evaluateTarget`. Unit tests in `lib/selection.test.ts`.
- `SelectionLine.astro` + `selection-line.ts` render `48 of 412 words selected` and `Cut these to land at 364 / 400 words <status>`. Selection is read from `#wc-text` on `select` and `selectionchange`, and stays out of the store and storage. Whitespace-only selections count as none. `usage.onSelectionCounted()` fires when the line shows.
- Not announced through a live region: selection changes are too chatty to speak.
- Speaking time left out (#21 not shipped). Added `unitLabel` to `lib/readout.ts`.
- Verified in a browser with Shift+arrows, `select()`, `setSelectionRange` and collapsing. Cmd/Ctrl+A in headless Chrome did not select the textarea, and touch selection on a real phone was not tried.

title: 29 · Session progress and writing sprints
description:
# 29 · Session progress and writing sprints

**Depends on:** #19, #20, #23
**Part of:** #17

## Why

So far every idea serves cutting. This one serves drafting: "+412 words this session" rewards sitting down to write, and a sprint timer gives people a reason to keep the tab open and come back.

## What

### Session progress

- Record the word count when the page loads (after restoring saved text, from #20).
- Show the change since then: `+412 this session`. Cutting shows as negative, framed positively, since cutting is progress in a second draft: `−86 this session (trimmed)`.
- Keep it in memory only. A reload starts a new session, so no new storage key is needed.

### Sprint timer

- A **Start a sprint** control with 10, 15, 25 minutes and a custom length.
- During a sprint, show time left and words written in this sprint. At the end, show a summary in the page: `25 minutes · 640 words`. No sound, and no notification permission prompt.
- The timer stays accurate in a background tab: compute from timestamps, not a counting interval.
- Respect `prefers-reduced-motion` for any countdown animation.
- Fire `wc_sprint_started { minutes }` and `wc_sprint_finished { minutes, word_bucket }` through the hooks #23 registered.

If #23's fake door for sprints is shipped first, use its results to decide whether to build the timer half of this ticket.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] Session progress shows the net change since load, including negative values.
- [x] A sprint's time left stays correct after the tab spends several minutes in the background.
- [x] Words written during a sprint exclude words that were already there.
- [x] The end-of-sprint summary is announced to screen readers.
- [x] No new storage keys are added.

## Outcome

Added `SessionPanel.astro` and `session-panel.ts`, mounted with one line in `main.ts` and one component in the page. Pure logic lives in `lib/session.ts` and `lib/sprint.ts` with unit tests.

- Session progress: baseline is the word count at mount (after saved text is restored), held in memory only. Shows `+412 this session`, `−86 this session (trimmed)`, or `No change this session`.
- Sprints: 10, 15, 25 minute buttons and a custom length (whole minutes, 1 to 180). Time left is computed from `Date.now()` timestamps on a 250ms tick and on `visibilitychange`, so it is right after a backgrounded tab wakes. The countdown bar only animates under `prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference`.
- Sprint words are the net change in word count since the sprint started, floored at 0. Deleting then retyping the same amount counts as 0, and cutting never shows a negative.
- The end-of-sprint summary (`25 minutes · 640 words`) is in a `role="status"` region, so it is announced. The ticking clock is a `role="timer"`, which is not announced.
- `usage.onSprintStarted` and `onSprintFinished` are called; a stopped sprint reports no finish. No new storage keys.
- Not verified: a real multi-minute background tab (the timer was checked by stubbing `Date.now`), screen reader output, and the final `[hidden]` CSS fix for the setup row was not re-checked in the browser after the edit.
- Later the same day, the sprint timer was taken out of the word counter and spun out into #31, a writing sprint tool of its own. The counter keeps session progress, now `SessionProgress.astro` and `session-progress.ts`. `lib/sprint.ts` and the `onSprintStarted` / `onSprintFinished` hooks were removed; #31 says where to find them in history.

title: 30 · Sentence rhythm strip
description:
# 30 · Sentence rhythm strip

**Depends on:** #18, #19, #20, #23
**Part of:** #17

## Why

Writers are told to vary sentence length, but it's hard to see in a block of text. A thin strip with one bar per sentence, scaled to its length, shows at a glance where prose drags (a run of long bars) or gets choppy (a run of short ones). It's the lightweight cousin of the "say-ability check" from the teleprompter brainstorm, and it makes the tool useful past the counting.

## What

- Split the text with #18's `sentences()`. It already handles abbreviations, ellipses, dialogue and line breaks, so this ticket is the strip and its interactions only.
- Draw one bar per sentence, in reading order, with height proportional to word count. Mark sentences over a threshold (start at 30 words) without relying on colour alone.
- Clicking or tapping a bar selects that sentence in the textarea and scrolls to it. Reuse the highlight component from #27 if it exists.
- A text summary for everyone, including screen readers: `24 sentences · average 17 words · longest 48 words`.
- The strip is collapsed by default, so the page stays simple for people who only want a count. Remember the choice in the `rhythmOpen` field #20 added to `wc:settings:v1`.
- Recompute only after typing settles, so long texts stay smooth.
- Fire `wc_rhythm_opened` and `wc_rhythm_sentence_clicked` through the hooks #23 registered.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] The strip uses #18's `sentences()`, with no sentence splitting of its own.
- [x] Bars match sentence lengths; clicking one selects that sentence.
- [x] Long sentences are marked by something other than colour.
- [x] The summary line is correct and readable by screen readers.
- [x] Typing stays smooth with 20,000 words and the strip open.

## Outcome

- `RhythmStrip.astro` and `rhythm-strip.ts` add one component and one `mountRhythmStrip(store, editor.highlights, usage)` line in `main.ts`. A disclosure button toggles `rhythmOpen` through the store (so `wc:settings:v1` remembers it) and fires `wc_rhythm_opened` on a user open, not on a restored one. Closing the strip clears its highlight.
- Pure logic is in `lib/rhythm.ts` with tests: summary (count, rounded average, longest, singular nouns), `LONG_SENTENCE_WORDS = 30`, per-sentence description, SVG path geometry, and pointer-to-bar mapping. Sentences come only from `sentences()`.
- **Rendering:** one SVG with three `<path>`s (normal bars, long bars, long marks), stretched with `preserveAspectRatio="none"`, so the cost doesn't grow with the number of sentences. A click is mapped to a bar from the pointer's position, so there is no element per bar. Bar height scales to the longest sentence, or to the threshold if no sentence reaches it.
- **Long sentences without colour:** a dashed threshold line that long bars rise past, a separate mark above each long bar, and the words "long sentence" in the detail line, plus a key under the strip.
- **Keyboard and screen readers:** the strip is one focus stop. Left/right/Home/End move a cursor, Enter or Space selects. A polite detail line reads `Sentence 2 of 3 · 4 words · “Four five six seven.”`. The summary line is plain text.
- **Selecting and scrolling:** the click paints a `sentence` highlight, focuses the textarea without scrolling, calls `setSelectionRange`, then `highlights.reveal("sentence")`. `reveal` is new in `lib/text-highlights.ts`: it renders the mirror at once, measures the first span's rectangle against the textarea's, and moves `scrollTop` just far enough (or to the span's top if it is taller than the textarea). Browsers disagree on whether setting the selection scrolls a textarea, so this measures instead. Checked scrolling both down and up.
- Recomputes 300 ms after typing settles. A click on a stale strip (text changed within that window) is ignored, so offsets never point at the wrong text. Any text change clears the sentence highlight.
- **Performance** (headless Chromium, dev server, 20,100 words in paragraphs, 1,675 sentences): a keystroke takes one frame (about 16.7 ms) with the strip closed and open. Opening, including splitting and drawing, took about 6 ms; `sentences()` itself about 3 ms.
- Verified in light, dark and highlighted themes, with keyboard navigation and clicks scrolling both ways. Not verified: Safari or Firefox, iOS touch, a screen reader, and forced-colors mode (styles written, not seen).
- Later removed from the word counter: sentence rhythm will be the first view of a writing analysis tool, #32. The strip, `lib/rhythm.ts`, `TextHighlights.reveal()`, the `rhythmOpen` setting and the rhythm hooks were removed; #32 says where to find them in history.

title: 31 · Writing sprint tool
description:
# 31 · Writing sprint tool

**Depends on:** #18, #23
**Part of:** #17 (spun out of #29)

## Why

#29 put a sprint timer in the word counter. In use, it didn't belong there. The counter is for getting a draft under a limit; a sprint is for getting words down in the first place. A sprint wants a focused writing screen, with the timer beside the text and nothing else competing, which fights with the counter's target, rhythm and selection panels. So sprints become their own tool, and the counter keeps only `+412 this session`.

## What

### Flow

- Choose a length: 10, 15 or 25 minutes, or a custom length. Then press **Start**, which sits below the choices rather than in the same row.
- **Start** focuses the text, so the writer can begin typing at once.
- While a sprint runs, the timer and its controls sit next to the text, not in a panel below it:
  - time left (the running word count is the one under the text);
  - **Pause** and resume;
  - **Stop**;
  - an eye toggle that hides the timer for writers who find it distracting, and shows it again. Hiding must not stop the sprint.
- At the end, show `25 minutes · 640 words` in the page and announce it to screen readers. No sound, and no notification permission prompt.

### Carried over from #29

The first version was built and then removed in the commit that created this ticket. `git show 6aa710c` has the parts worth reusing:

- `src/tools/word-counter/lib/sprint.ts` and its tests: time left from timestamps (right after a backgrounded tab wakes), sprint words as the net change since the start floored at 0, the clock and summary text.
- A 250ms re-render plus `visibilitychange`, never a counting interval.
- Count with `src/lib/text/measure.ts`, so numbers match the word counter and teleprompter.
- The countdown bar animates only under `prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference`.

Pause needs the timer model to grow: time left must be based on elapsed running time, not wall time since the start.

### A new tool

- Lay it out like the other tools: `src/tools/writing-sprint/` with a store and a mount function per part, and a page in `src/pages/tools/` that only composes components. Add it to the tools index.
- Decide whether the text is saved between visits. If it is, that's a new storage key in the privacy registry; reuse the word counter's approach (#20).
- Analytics: `wc_sprint_started` and `wc_sprint_finished` are still in `EVENT_SCHEMA` and the lock, but nothing fires them since they left the word counter. Replace them with events named for this tool, and remove the `wc_sprint_*` pair, in one `npm run privacy:lock` bump. Until then, the privacy policy lists two events that never fire.
- Run the `privacy-reviewer` agent, since this adds a tool under `src/tools`.
- Consider an "open in word counter" hand-off for the finished draft, the way #22 links the counter to the teleprompter.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] Start sits below the length choices and focuses the text.
- [x] The timer, pause, stop and hide controls sit next to the text while a sprint runs.
- [x] Hiding the timer doesn't stop or pause the sprint.
- [x] Pause and resume keep time left correct, including across a backgrounded tab.
- [x] Words written during a sprint exclude words that were already there.
- [x] The end-of-sprint summary is announced to screen readers.
- [x] The `wc_sprint_*` events are replaced in the schema and lock, and the privacy policy lists only events that fire.

## Outcome

- Built as `src/tools/writing-sprint/` at `/tools/writing-sprint`, listed on the tools index. Setup (10, 15, 25 or custom minutes, with **Start** below) swaps for a bar above the text with time left, **Pause**/**Resume**, **Stop** and a hide-timer toggle. Start focuses the text.
- The timer model grew pause: time left comes from running time only (`elapsedBeforePauseMs` plus the current stretch), so pausing and a backgrounded tab both stay correct. Tests cover each.
- The draft is saved under its own key, `ws:text`, separate from the word counter's `wc:text`.
- A light word count sits under the text. There is no hand-off to the word counter; #32 (the writing analysis tool) takes the finished draft instead.
- `wc_sprint_*` became `ws_sprint_started` and `ws_sprint_finished`, with the new storage key, in one lock bump to 2.3.0. The privacy scan now types into this tool too.

title: 32 · Writing analysis tool
description:
# 32 · Writing analysis tool

**Depends on:** #18, #23
**Part of:** #17 (spun out of #30)

## Why

#30 put a sentence rhythm strip in the word counter. It was useful, but it's one view of a bigger job: looking at how a draft reads, not just how long it is. That job deserves its own tool with room for several views. The word counter can then stay focused on getting a draft to a limit.

## What

- A tool for looking at a draft as writing. Sentence rhythm is the first view. Candidates for later views include long and short sentence runs, paragraph lengths, repeated words, and reading or speaking time per section.
- Lay it out like the other tools: `src/tools/<name>/` with a store and a mount function per part, and a page in `src/pages/tools/` that only composes components. Add it to the tools index.
- Use #18's `sentences()` and `measure()`, so its numbers match the word counter and teleprompter.

### Carried over from #30

The rhythm strip was built and then removed in the commit that created this ticket. `git show 0256dc3` has the parts worth reusing:

- `src/tools/word-counter/lib/rhythm.ts` and its tests: the summary line, the long-sentence threshold, and SVG geometry that draws thousands of sentences as three paths.
- `src/tools/word-counter/rhythm-strip.ts`: pointer and keyboard selection of a bar, and recomputing only after typing settles. It stayed within one frame per keystroke at 20,000 words.
- `TextHighlights.reveal(kind)` in `src/lib/text-highlights.ts`: scrolls the textarea to a painted span. It was removed with the strip; restore it if the tool selects text in a textarea.

### Analytics and privacy

- `wc_rhythm_opened` and `wc_rhythm_sentence_clicked` are still in `EVENT_SCHEMA` and the lock, but nothing fires them. Replace them with events named for this tool, in one `npm run privacy:lock` bump. Until then, the privacy policy lists two events that never fire.
- Run the `privacy-reviewer` agent, since this adds a tool under `src/tools`.

### Static analysis, and the sprint hand-off

This is an analysis tool, not a drafting tool. Text arrives by paste, by hand-off or from the last visit, so recompute after input settles rather than optimising keystrokes.

When a writing sprint (#31) finishes, a link beside its word count opens this tool with the draft. The draft travels in the URL hash (the teleprompter's share payload, origin `writing_sprint`), so it never reaches a server.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] The tool shows sentence rhythm for pasted or typed text, using #18's `sentences()`.
- [x] 20,000 words analyse without freezing the page.
- [x] The `wc_rhythm_*` events are replaced in the schema and lock, and the privacy policy lists only events that fire.
- [x] Finishing a sprint shows a link beside the word count that opens this tool with the draft. Stopping or restarting a sprint hides it.

## Outcome

- Added Draft Analysis at `/tools/draft-analysis` (`src/tools/draft-analysis/`), with the sentence rhythm strip restored from `0256dc3` and always shown. `TextHighlights.reveal()` is back.
- The Writing Sprint shows "See analytics on your draft" beside its word count once a sprint finishes. The draft travels in the URL hash using the teleprompter's share payload, with a new `writing_sprint` origin.
- `wc_rhythm_*` events are replaced by `da_text_entered`, `da_rhythm_sentence_clicked` and `ws_opened_analysis`. Registry lock is 2.4.0, with a new `da:text` storage key.
- The privacy scan now types into the tool and follows the sprint hand-off, so it can catch a leak of the draft.
- Later views (paragraph lengths, repeated words, reading time per section) are not built.

title: 33 · Magic 8 Ball
description:
# 33 · Magic 8 Ball

**Depends on:** #23

## Why

A lighter tool, for fun: something to ask when a draft (or anything else) needs a nudge. It's a chance to make a more immersive page than the writing tools, and it brings search traffic for "magic 8 ball online" to the site.

## What

- A 3D Magic 8 Ball at `/tools/magic-8-ball`. The ball is modelled in Blender by `scripts/models/magic-8-ball.py` and drawn by a small WebGL2 renderer of our own (`ball-webgl.ts`). It shades each material with a matcap: a picture of a sphere in that material, in `public/models/magic-8-ball-matcaps.webp`. The matcaps were baked once from the three.js renderer at commit 0e57180, which is the source of the look; changing the shine means re-baking from there. Each 256 px cell is a unit sphere in one material with that commit's lights, environment and tone mapping and no fog. It's seen from the page camera's distance with the sphere filling the cell, except the rim cell, which is seen head-on. The atlas is saved as WebP at quality 92 with sharp YUV. A CSS ball stands in while the model loads, and stays if WebGL2 or the model isn't available.
- Both balls first show their 8 for a beat, then turn to the window. The die tumbles in blue water while the ball is shaken and rises clear of the haze to answer.
- An optional question. You can shake the ball four ways: submit the question, click or press a key on the ball, drag it back and forth, or shake your phone. iOS asks for motion access from a tap first.
- Two decks: the classic 20 answers, and a writer's deck in the Department's voice.
- Shaking again before the answer settles clouds the window and gives a hazy answer.
- A log of this visit's questions and answers, in memory only.
- A share dialog that copies, shares or downloads an image of the question and answer.
- A full-bleed dark scene under the site header, with the usual SEO article and FAQ below.

### Analytics and privacy

- `m8_shaken`, `m8_shared` and `m8_motion_permission`, which never carry the question or answer. Added in one `npm run privacy:lock` bump.
- Nothing is saved, so no new storage keys.
- The phone's motion is read only in the page, to notice a shake.
- Run the `privacy-reviewer` agent, since this adds a tool under `src/tools`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] Each of the four ways of shaking gives an answer, and a slow drag doesn't count as a shake.
- [x] Shaking during settling gives a hazy answer.
- [x] The answer is announced to screen readers, and the ball works from the keyboard.
- [x] Reduced motion drops the tumbling and sloshing, and the answer cross-fades in.
- [x] Without WebGL, the CSS ball still answers.
- [x] The share image copies where the browser allows it, and downloads everywhere.
- [x] No CSP violations, and the privacy scan passes with the tool included.
- [ ] Shaking a real phone works on iOS and Android.

title: 34 · Turn on enhanced measurement and describe events by category
description:
# 34 · Turn on enhanced measurement and describe events by category

**Depends on:** #14

## Why

`privacy/google-analytics.md` kept enhanced measurement off because it adds automatic events that weren't in our event schema, and the privacy policy promised "The exact events we send". GDPR and ePrivacy require us to describe the categories of data we collect and why, not to list every event name. The exact list was a choice we made, and it blocked a feature we want.

Enhanced measurement is configured in the GA admin, not in code, so without a guard nothing would notice a toggle being flipped there.

## What

1. Declare the events Google sends itself in `AUTOMATIC_EVENT_SCHEMA` (`src/lib/analytics/events.ts`), separate from `EVENT_SCHEMA` so `track()` can't send them. Lock both together (`LOCKED_ANALYTICS_SCHEMA`), so the lock's bump rules and Jev review them like our own events.
2. The privacy scan fails on any `/g/collect` hit whose event name isn't in the lock, both on page scans and on the tool runs that type the sentinel. It scrolls each page to the bottom so `scroll` is exercised. GA holds hits for about five seconds, so the scan hides the page before reading requests, which makes GA send them as it would when a visitor leaves.
3. Remove "The exact events we send" from the privacy policy. Describe the automatic events in plain language in the Analytics section.
4. Update `privacy/google-analytics.md`, `privacy/vendors.md` and `privacy/processing-record.md`.
5. In the GA admin, set enhanced measurement the same on the production and test properties: scrolls, outbound clicks, form interactions, site search, video engagement and file downloads on, and history-based page views off.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] Automatic events declared and locked (minor bump, no re-consent: the purpose is unchanged).
- [x] Scan rejects undeclared analytics events.
- [x] The privacy policy describes events by category, with no exact event list.
- [x] Records in `privacy/` match the policy and the lock.
- [x] Enhanced measurement set in both properties, and its checklist item in `privacy/google-analytics.md` ticked with the date.
- [x] `npm run privacy:scan` passes with the toggles on, and the accepted state's hits include `scroll`.
- [x] History page views off: the tag served for both properties shows `"vtp_enableHistoryEvents":false`.
- [x] User-provided data collection off for both properties, including automatic detection in each Google tag's settings.

## Findings along the way

- Before the scan hid the page, it read requests about 300ms after each flow, while GA sends batched hits after about five seconds. Most analytics hits, including the tools' own events, never reached its sentinel and declaration checks. With the flush, a scan whose lock had every event removed reported `scroll` on all 13 pages, plus `user_engagement`, `m8_shaken`, `da_*`, `tp_*`, `wc_target_set` and `ws_sprint_started`. The real scan still passes, so none of those hits carried visitor text.
- After history events were unticked in the admin, the tag served for both properties still has `"vtp_enableHistoryEvents":true`. It changed to `false` later the same day, so admin changes take a while to reach the served tag.
- The served tag also includes `__ogt_1p_data_v2` with automatic email, phone and address detection, although user-provided data collection was off in both properties: automatic detection is a separate switch in each Google tag's settings. A probe that typed an email address and phone number into the Magic 8 Ball question sent nothing email- or phone-like to Google. The switch was turned off on both tags the same day, and the served tags now show `"vtp_isAutoEnabled":false`.

## Outcome

Enhanced measurement is on in both properties (2026-10-16), with history page views off. `AUTOMATIC_EVENT_SCHEMA` declares the events Google sends itself. `LOCKED_ANALYTICS_SCHEMA` locks them with the site's own events, rather than in a separate section of the lock, so the bump rules, Jev and the scan treat them the same (lock 2.6.0, minor). Jev's flags on `form_submit_text`, `search_term`, `file_name` and `video_title` were checked against the code and accepted. The privacy policy now describes the automatic events in plain language instead of listing every event. The scan rejects undeclared events and flushes GA's batched hits before reading requests.

Follow-ups from the privacy review, done the next day:
- The cookie policy mentions scroll depth and outbound clicks.
- The review suggested site search couldn't collect terms because `page_location` has no query string. A probe showed it does: GA reads the real page URL, and `/blog/?q=probe-search-term` sent `ep.search_term=probe-search-term`. The site has no search, so site search is now off on both streams and `view_search_results` is removed from the lock (2.7.0, minor). The scan loads `/blog/?q=scan-search-query` and fails if it comes back on. The privacy reviewer agent asks about turning it back on whenever a diff adds site search.
- The scan report records the analytics event names each page sent.

title: 36 · Continuity Checker coming soon page
description:
# 36 · Continuity Checker coming soon page

**Depends on:** #37. This branch stays unmerged until the form exists, so the page can't deploy with its buttons pointing at `#`.
**Part of:** —

## Why

The Continuity Checker will be our first paid tool. The spike in `spike-manuscript-continuity` (`CONCLUSION.md`) found it ready to build: a strong second pair of eyes, not a guarantee. Before we build it, we want to know who wants it, what they write, and what they'd pay. A coming soon page at the tool's own URL lets us find out, and the same URL becomes the tool when it ships.

## What

- **Tools index:** list the Continuity Checker with a Soon tag. The Soon pill moves out of the teleprompter's fake doors into a shared `SoonTag` component. The lede drops "free", since not every tool will be.
- **`/tools/continuity-checker`:**
  - a hero with the headline "Catch it before your reader does" and a Join the waitlist button;
  - three example flags on a sample story (the door in the hill), in the shape the spike's output takes: sure or maybe, both passages quoted, a one-line reason;
  - what it checks, and why it's different;
  - where your manuscript goes;
  - a closing Highlighted band with a second button.
- **Claims:** only the ones `CONCLUSION.md` says we can make. Never "catches every error", a percentage, "replaces your editor", or anything about who knows what.
- **Payment:** not mentioned on the page.

title: 37 · Waitlist form for the Continuity Checker
description:
# 37 · Waitlist form for the Continuity Checker

**Depends on:** —
**Part of:** #36
**Numbered #34 before the move to beads:** commits on this branch from before the move cite it as #34.

## Why

The coming soon page (#36) exists to collect a waitlist and learn from the writers who join it. Collecting email addresses changes what the privacy policy can promise, so how we collect them is a decision to make deliberately.

## Decisions

- **Our own form, posting to a Cloudflare Worker with a D1 database created with `--jurisdiction eu`.** Typeform was ruled out: its free plan allows about 10 responses a month and it stores data in the US. A Tally link would look like Tally and keep the visitor off our page, and a Tally embed loads a third party on page load. Supabase's free projects pause after a week without activity.
- **The Worker is served from `*.workers.dev`.** DNS is at GoDaddy, and a custom domain needs the zone on Cloudflare. If DNS moves later, changing the origin in `VENDORS` is enough.
- **One endpoint and one policy for every form.** Each submission records which form it came from and, where relevant, the feature (`continuity-checker`, `teleprompter:voice_scroll`), so we only email people about what they asked about. The privacy policy's "Waitlists and forms" section covers forms in general, and each form states its own purpose next to its button. Accounts are out of scope (#15).
- **The teleprompter's coming-soon email signup ships in this release.** Fill in `subscribe()` in `src/tools/teleprompter/lib/interest.ts`, then remove `EMAIL_CAPTURE_ENABLED`.
- **Form order:** step 1 is the email and consent boxes, saved straight away. Step 2, "Help us build it", holds Q1–Q10, all optional.
- **Retention:** a submission, email and answers together, is kept until we've sent what the person asked for. If we decide not to build it, we tell them and delete it then. They can ask us to delete it sooner. There's no time-based clean-up, so nothing needs running on a schedule.
- **Sending:** by hand from our Proton Mail inbox, in batches of up to 100 BCC recipients. Unsubscribing means replying, and we act on the reply. Proton isn't recorded in this release; add a `privacy/vendors.md` section before the first send (Swiss, so EU adequacy covers transfers). The policy names "our email provider" as a category of recipient so it stays true in the meantime.
- **New UI:** add `ChoiceField` (radio or checkbox options) and `ScaleField` (1–5) next to `TextField.astro`. Write the survey as plain Astro markup, with no form schema or rendering engine.
- **Consent on the form:** pressing "Email me when it launches" is the consent to the launch email, so there's no required checkbox. "I'd like to try an early version" is an optional box, unticked by default, for inviting beta testers. Each form names its own purpose next to its button and links to the privacy policy.
- **No confirmation email.** The Worker can't send mail. The first email we send says why the person is getting it and how to be removed.
- **Answers aren't published or quoted without asking first.** The policy promises this for every form.
- **Storage is one `submissions` table**, not Workers Logs. Logs are kept for only 3–7 days and can't be deleted entry by entry, and turning them on would record the IP addresses the policy says we don't keep. The Worker has logging turned off (`observability.enabled: false`).
- **Delete whole rows.** The email and answers share a row, so after sending, delete that form's rows rather than clearing columns.

## Progress

Done, in commits `a7f63b0` and `6a3e164`:

- **Cloudflare:** the account exists and wrangler is logged in. The D1 database `forms` was created in the `eu` jurisdiction (id in `workers/forms/wrangler.jsonc`), and the free plan allows it. The live database has no tables yet.
- **Policy and records:** the privacy policy has its "Waitlists and forms" section, and `privacy/processing-record.md` has a matching entry.
- **Worker:** `workers/forms/index.ts` handles `POST /signups` (returns `{ id }`) and `POST /answers` (`{ signupId, answers }`, accepted once per signup). It checks the origin and body size, rate-limits to 10 requests a minute per IP (the IP is never stored), and quietly drops honeypot submissions.
- **Schema:** `workers/forms/migrations/0001_create_submissions.sql`.
- **Shared validation:** `src/lib/forms/submission.ts`, with tests. The forms should validate with it too.
- **Scripts:**
  - `npm run forms:dev` runs the Worker and a local database at `localhost:8787` and accepts requests from `localhost:4321`.
  - `npm run forms:deploy` applies migrations to the live database, then deploys.

Form work, tested end to end against `npm run forms:dev`:

- **Worker address:** `PUBLIC_FORMS_URL` in `src/env.d.ts`, set to `http://localhost:8787` in `public-env/.env.development`. The production value goes in `public-env/.env.production` after the first deploy. The public-env test now covers every file in the folder.
- **Client:** `src/lib/forms/client.ts` (`sendSignup`, `sendSurveyAnswers`) and `src/lib/forms/answers.ts` (`readAnswers`, which turns a survey form into `Answers`).
- **Fields:** `ChoiceField` and `ScaleField`, with READMEs in `design-system/components/` and sandbox pages. They aren't in the React bundle.
- **Form:** `/tools/continuity-checker/waitlist/` (`src/tools/continuity-checker/WaitlistForm.astro` and `waitlist-form.ts`). Both Join the waitlist buttons link to it. The privacy policy's section now has the anchor `#waitlists-and-forms`.
- **Astro's CSP isn't applied in dev**, so the form reaches localhost there. A production build blocks the Worker until the Cloudflare `VENDORS` entry (step 6) adds its origin to `connect-src`.

**Not deployed yet, on purpose.** Everything can be tested end to end locally with `npm run forms:dev` and `npm run dev`. Deploy once, before the site deploys. That first deploy is also what reveals the production URL, `forms.<subdomain>.workers.dev`.

## Next steps

1. **Moved to #39:** the maintenance scripts, deferred until we first need them.
2. **Done:** the site setting, client, field components and the Continuity Checker form. See Progress.
5. **Done:** the teleprompter's coming-soon dialog saves an optional email as `teleprompter:<feature>`, only when the visitor answers "Yes". It names the feature, links to the policy, and shows a problem when the email is incomplete or can't be saved. `EMAIL_CAPTURE_ENABLED` and `lib/interest.ts` are gone.
6. **Done:** the `forms` category and Cloudflare vendor in the registry, the `privacy/vendors.md` section, `PUBLIC_FORMS_URL` in `.env.production`, and both forms in the pre-deploy scan. `npm run privacy:lock` wrote 2.6.0 with Cloudflare's processor role confirmed.
7. **Done:** the `privacy-reviewer` pass. Fixed: forms post rather than put values in the URL when their script hasn't loaded; the honeypot is `reference_code` instead of the autofilled `website`; the survey links to the policy; the Worker returns 409 when answers match no signup; the scan flags a request to the Worker when nothing was submitted; the cookie policy, `processing-record.md` and `vendors.md` wording on transfers, logs and unverified consent.
8. **Done:** shipped with #36 in the deploy of `64ddc09` on 2026-10-18. The Worker is at `https://forms.seconddrafts.workers.dev` (redeploy with `npm run forms:deploy` after changing it), and a signup from the live site reached the live database.

## What

Common to every form option (a subset of #15):

- **Privacy policy:** drafted. "What we don't do" now carves out forms, and a new "Waitlists and forms" section covers purpose, legal basis, recipients, retention and how to be removed.
- **Records:** `privacy/processing-record.md` drafted. Still to do: the Cloudflare section in `privacy/vendors.md`.
- **Email guard:** the test that asserted `EMAIL_CAPTURE_ENABLED` is false has been removed, because the policy now covers the teleprompter signup.
- **Review:** run the `privacy-reviewer` agent.
- **Survey free text:** Q6 and the Q10 reassurance box invite quotes from manuscripts. The policy now covers this, and the form's hint should say there's no need to paste passages.
- **One consent per purpose:** launch email, early access, and using answers for product research are separate purposes. Each needs its own legal basis and wording, and withdrawing must be as easy as agreeing.
- **Analytics:** keep `cc_waitlist_clicked` count-only. Never add an event carrying form values or the email address.

For our own form:

- **Worker:** a POST endpoint with CORS limited to `https://seconddrafts.com`, a honeypot field and a rate limit. No Turnstile, since it's another third-party script. Deploy it with its own npm script, separate from `deploy`.
- **Operations:** npm scripts to export signups (for sending the launch email), to delete a form's rows once we've sent its email, and to delete one person by email (for removal requests).
- **Records:** a `VENDORS` entry for Cloudflare, with the Worker origin in `origins.data`. That feeds `connect-src`, and `form-action` stays `'self'` because we submit with `fetch`. Its role is processor and its transfer basis is the EU–US Data Privacy Framework. Add a section in `privacy/vendors.md` for Cloudflare. `privacy:lock` needs a person to confirm Cloudflare's role, and `privacy:records` needs its terms recorded.
- **Leak checks:** add both forms to `TOOLS_VISITORS_WRITE_IN` in `scripts/privacy-scan.ts`. Answers may reach our Worker's origin and must go nowhere else.
- **No IP addresses in storage:** the policy promises we don't store them with a submission. The rate limit may use the IP in memory, but never write it to D1.
- **Errors:** if the save fails, show a clear message and offer emailing us as a fallback.

### Survey questions

1. What are you working on? (novel / series / short fiction / screenplay / narrative nonfiction / other)
2. Genre?
3. How long is it? (under 50k words / 50–100k / 100–150k / 150k+ / a series)
4. Where is it now? (first draft / revising / going to readers, an agent or an editor soon / published)
5. How do you catch continuity slips today? (memory / notes or a story bible / beta readers / an editor / software / I don't)
6. Tell us about a slip you or a reader caught. (open text)
7. When would you run a check? (after each session / before it goes to readers / both)
8. What do you write in? (Word / Google Docs / Scrivener / Markdown or plain text / other). The spike only reads plain text.
9. What would you expect to pay to check one full manuscript? (price bands / I'd want a subscription / I wouldn't pay)
10. How do you feel about sending your manuscript to an AI service for checking? (1–5, plus an optional "what would reassure you?")
11. Moved to step 1: the email field and an optional "I'd like to try an early version" box. The button wording carries the launch-email consent.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] Tool chosen and retention decided.
- [x] Privacy policy, records and email guard updated in the same release as the form.
- [x] Both Join the waitlist buttons lead to the form. `WAITLIST_URL` in `src/tools/continuity-checker/waitlist.ts` is replaced or points at it.
- [x] The teleprompter's coming-soon email signup saves to the same Worker.
- [x] The Worker is deployed, and a signup from the live site reaches the live database.
- [x] `npm run predeploy` passes.

title: 39 · Forms maintenance scripts
description:
# 39 · Forms maintenance scripts

**Depends on:** —
**Follows:** #37

## Why

The privacy policy promises we keep a form submission, email and answers together, until we've sent what the person asked for, delete it if we decide not to build what they asked about, and delete it sooner on request. Today that means running SQL by hand in the D1 console. Write the scripts when we first need them: before the first launch email, or at the first removal request.

## What

npm scripts that wrap `wrangler d1 execute forms --remote -c workers/forms/wrangler.jsonc`:

- Export one form's emails, comma-separated in groups of 100 for BCC (we send by hand from Proton Mail). Record the time of the export.
- After sending, delete that form's rows created up to the export time, so later signups aren't removed. Do the same for a form whose tool we decide not to build, after telling those people.
- Delete everything for one email, for removal requests.

Print counts, never the emails themselves, except in the export, which writes to a file outside the repo.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The three scripts exist and are documented in `package.json`.
- [ ] Proton Mail has a section in `privacy/vendors.md` before the first send.
